item.title: Hesiod, the Theogony, and Our Oedipal Wounds — On Myths That Know Us Better Than We Know Ourselves
item.description:
To Nevzat Kaya, thank you for inspiring me!

He pulled me out of a room where intelligence worshipped itself, where STEM had already decided what counted as knowing (STEM elitism kills the wonder!).

He reminded me that I am human first: a hungry animal, thirsty for story, for myths, for everything the equations leave out!

I do not know how to thank him enough. Endless thanks.

Before there was anything, there was Chaos.

The word does not mean disorder. It means something more precise: the primordial gap, the yawning abyss, the opened mouth of nothingness.

Χάος — Kháos.

From this opening, everything comes.

Gaia, the deep-breasted earth.

Tartarus, the dark pit beneath the earth.

Eros: desire, the force that makes things reach toward each other.

Erebus, darkness. Night.

And from Night: Day.

From Darkness: Space.

Hesiod begins this way — not with a god who creates, but with a gap that opens, and from the opening, generation.

The universe does not begin with intention. It begins with an absence that cannot sustain itself, that generates in order to fill itself, that produces the world as a consequence of its own incompleteness.

I want to argue this is not only a cosmogony.

It is the deepest description we have of what it is to be human.

I. Hesiod and the Theogony

Hesiod was a Greek poet! Contemporary with Homer, perhaps slightly later, perhaps slightly earlier.

He came from Ascra, in Boeotia which is a small farming village, not the heroic world of the Homeric epics.

Where Homer wrote about warriors and kings, the world of kleos, glory, the great deed, Hesiod wrote about farmers, laborers, the grinding difficulty of ordinary life.

He wrote two major poems that survive:

Works and Days: a poem of practical instruction, addressed to his brother Perses, about farming, justice, and the rhythms of the year.

Theogony: the birth of the gods, the genealogy of the cosmos, the account of how everything came to be.

The Theogony is our source for the systematic Greek cosmogony. The account of origins that shaped Western thought from the pre-Socratics through Plato through Ovid through Milton through Freud.

At roughly a thousand lines, it is the founding document of Western mythology.

II. The Violence at the Origin

What the Theogony tells us, relentlessly, is that creation requires violence.

Not violence as accident. Violence as structure.

Ouranos, the Sky, mates with Gaia, the Earth, but refuses to let his children be born. He pushes them back into their mother as they emerge.

Gaia, in agony, fashions a great sickle and asks her children to castrate their father.

Only Kronos agrees.

He castrates Ouranos. The severed genitals fall into the sea. From the foam, aphros, that gathers around them, Aphrodite is born.

From the blood that falls on the earth: the Giants, the Furies, the ash-tree Nymphs.

Creation from dismemberment. Beauty from castration. The goddess of love born from an act of violence.

The Theogony states this outright, as its central argument:

The world as it is required the destruction of what was.

Every generation of gods comes to power by overthrowing the previous generation.

Ouranos is castrated by Kronos. Kronos swallows his own children to prevent them from overthrowing him, because Ouranos and Gaia have prophesied that he will be overthrown by his son.

Zeus, hidden by his mother Rhea, forces Kronos to vomit up his siblings, defeats the Titans in the Titanomachy, and establishes the current order.

The current order, our world, the world we inhabit, is built on a foundation of successive violations.

Father castrated by son. Children swallowed by father. Father defeated by son.

More than myth, it is the structure of time itself, the new requiring the destruction of the old, the future feeding on the past, every generation haunted by what it had to do to become itself.

III. Kronos and the Devouring Father

Kronos swallows his children!

Hestia. Demeter. Hera. Hades. Poseidon. Each one, as born, taken from Rhea’s arms and swallowed.

Why?

Because the oracle said his son would overthrow him as he overthrew his father.

He knows what he is. He knows what he did. He knows what will be done to him.

And so he swallows his children! Not from malice, but from fear! From the terror of the inevitable…

Here the Theogony reaches its most psychologically precise moment.

The father who destroys his children is not a monster. He is a man who knows history, who knows that the structure of time requires his replacement, and who cannot bear it.

He swallows them to stop time. To prevent the future from happening. To remain the sovereign of the present by eliminating those who would make him the past.

It does not work!

It never works!

Zeus is hidden. Zeus grows. Zeus returns. The swallowed children are vomited up. Kronos is defeated!

The future cannot be swallowed. It can only be delayed and the delay makes it more violent when it finally comes!

IV. Zeus and the New Order

Zeus wins!

He defeats the Titans. He defeats Typhon. He establishes the Olympian order, assigns domains to gods, marries Hera, produces an extraordinary number of children through an extraordinary number of liaisons.

Zeus is not a gentle god.

He rules through power, through the thunderbolt, through the threat of force, through the reminder that he has defeated everyone who challenged him!

But he also rules through intelligence, mêtis, a quality so important that he swallows the goddess Metis when she is pregnant with Athena, because the oracle says that Metis will bear a child greater than the father.

He cannot let that happen. So he swallows Metis, and Athena is born from his head, fully formed, in armor.

Wisdom born from the inside of the sovereign’s skull. Intelligence that belongs entirely to power, that cannot exist outside it, that is born through the sovereign’s self-cannibalism.

Notice the repetition:

Ouranos prevents birth. Kronos swallows children. Zeus swallows the mother of his most important child.

Each generation finds a new way to try to stop the next generation.

Each fails!

Because the structure of time cannot be stopped: only deformed.

V. The Oedipal Structure

Freud named his most famous complex after Oedipus.

This has been so thoroughly absorbed into culture that we have forgotten how strange it is: how much it both illuminates and distorts what Sophocles actually wrote.

Freud’s Oedipus complex: the child desires the parent of the opposite sex, fears castration (or its equivalent) from the same-sex parent, and eventually resolves this through identification with the same-sex parent and renunciation of the desire.

A story, at bottom, about desire and its renunciation, about the child’s entry into the social order through the abandonment of an impossible wish.

Sophocles’s Oedipus is something different.

Oedipus kills his father and sleeps with his mother, but he does not know it.

The horror of Oedipus Rex is not desire. It is knowledge.

Oedipus is the man who will not stop asking.

Warned by Tiresias to stop the investigation, told, effectively, that the answer will destroy him, he continues.

“I will not listen. I must know the truth.”

He finds out. He knows. He puts out his own eyes.

Why does he blind himself?

Not as punishment for the incest, which was unknowing, but because the eyes that saw but could not see are no longer worthy of the light.

He was blind when he could see. Now he will be blind without pretense.

VI. Oedipus as Epistemological Hero

Here is the reading that mythology gives us that psychology obscures:

Oedipus is not primarily about desire. He is about the will to know, and what knowing costs.

He is the detective, the first detective in Western literature, who will not stop investigating even when the investigation leads to himself.

He is the scientist who will not falsify data to protect a comfortable conclusion.

He is the philosopher who follows the argument wherever it leads, including to the place where it destroys the philosopher’s own foundations.

“I must know the truth.” This is not hubris in the conventional sense. Call it intellectual courage, of the deepest kind: the willingness to be the object of your own investigation, the refusal to grant yourself exemption from the questions you ask of others.

Oedipus is destroyed by truth. He would not have had it otherwise.

There is something in this that resonates beyond Greek tragedy.

Every serious intellectual, every person who has followed an argument to its uncomfortable conclusion, who has found themselves implicated in what they set out to investigate, who has discovered that the questioner is part of the question, has been Oedipus.

The willingness to put out your own eyes rather than unsee what you have seen. This is not pathology. Call it honesty, in its most demanding form.

VII. The Hesiodic and the Oedipal — Together

What connects Hesiod’s cosmogony to Sophocles’s tragedy?

Both are stories about the violence of origins, about what must be destroyed for anything to come into being.

In Hesiod: the cosmos requires castration, swallowing, defeat. The world as it is is built on the ruins of what it destroyed to become itself.

In Sophocles: knowledge requires the destruction of the self that did not know. The Oedipus who knows at the end of the play is not the Oedipus who began it. He has been destroyed and remade, at the cost of his eyes, his throne, his family, his city.

Both stories say: you cannot become without destruction.

The cosmos cannot be born without the father being unmade.

The truth cannot be known without the knower being transformed by what they learn.

The deepest mythological wisdom is this:

Origin is violence. Knowledge is violence. Becoming is violence, not in the sense of cruelty, but in the sense of irreversibility.

What has been destroyed to make you cannot be restored.

The eyes that saw Ouranos castrated, the ears that heard the oracle, cannot unremember.

The only question is: what do you do with the irreversibility?

VIII. The Mythological Answer

Greek mythology does not offer comfort.

It does not say: the violence was worth it. It does not say: everything happens for a reason. It does not say: the suffering will be redeemed.

It says: this is the structure of things.

Chaos opens. Generation begins. Each generation destroys and is destroyed. The cosmos is built on castration. Knowledge is built on self-blinding. The order we inhabit is the product of violences we did not choose and cannot undo.

And we live here. In this order. With these origins. Carrying these wounds.

The Theogony does not ask us to overcome our origins. It asks us to know them.

Oedipus does not ask us to avoid the truth. It asks us to follow it, wherever it leads, including into darkness.

Here, then, is the mythological answer:

Not redemption. Recognition.

The courageous act is not to transcend the violence at the origin of things. It is to look at it clearly, with eyes that have earned their sight through the willingness to see, and say:

Yes. This is where I come from. This is what made me. I know it now. I will not look away.

IX. What We Carry

We are all Oedipal in the mythological sense, not in Freud’s narrower sense, but in the sense that Sophocles intended:

We are all the products of origins we did not choose and cannot fully know.

We are all carrying wounds inflicted before we could consent to them: family wounds, cultural wounds, historical wounds, the wounds of being born into a specific time and place and body.

And we are all, like Oedipus, confronted with the choice:

To stop asking. To accept the comfortable not-knowing. To live in the city of Thebes without looking too closely at how it was built.

Or to ask. To follow the question. To risk what Oedipus risked, the discovery that the investigator is implicated in what they investigate, that the wound and the healer are the same person, that knowing changes nothing about what happened and everything about who you are in relation to what happened.

Tiresias warned Oedipus. He did not listen.

I think Sophocles admired him for it.

I do too.

X. Hesiod’s Last Word

The Theogony ends not with resolution but with catalogue: the endless list of gods and their children, the proliferation of divine genealogy that is the cosmos’s way of sustaining itself through multiplication.

There is something honest about this ending.

The cosmos does not resolve. It generates. It continues. It produces more of itself: more gods, more heroes, more stories, more attempts to understand the original gap that opened before anything was.

Chaos — the first word. The gap that is not nothing but the condition of everything.

We come from this.

Not from order, not from intention, not from a god who shaped us with a clear purpose in mind —

but from an opening, a gap, an abyss that could not sustain its own emptiness and began, from that unbearable fullness of nothing, to generate.

We are the cosmos knowing itself.

Imperfectly. Painfully. With eyes that sometimes need to be put out before they can truly see.

But knowing.

That is what we are. That is what we do.

That is, perhaps, enough.

Further reading:

Hesiod — Theogony and Works and Days (trans. M.L. West — Oxford World’s Classics)

Sophocles — The Three Theban Plays (trans. Robert Fagles — Penguin Classics)

Walter Burkert — Greek Religion (1985) — the essential scholarly introduction

Jean-Pierre Vernant — Myth and Thought Among the Greeks (1983) — the best structural analysis of Greek mythology

Bernard Knox — The Heroic Temper (1964) — on Oedipus and the will to know

Roberto Calasso — The Marriage of Cadmus and Harmony (1993) — mythology as literature; the most beautiful book about Greek myth

item.title: The Problem of the Self: Does "You" Exist?
item.description:
You are reading this sentence.

Behind your eyes, something is happening, a process, an experience, a witnessing. There is, it seems, a you doing the reading.

This seems like the most obvious fact in the world. Descartes built his entire philosophy on it: cogito ergo sum, I think, therefore I am.

The I is the one thing we cannot doubt.

I want to suggest that Descartes was wrong. Not about the thinking, about the I.

Hume’s Bundle Theory

In 1739, David Hume sat down and tried to introspect on his own self.

He expected to find, as most people assume, some stable, continuous entity. The “I” that persists through time. The subject of all experience.

What he found instead:

“When I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other, of heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain or pleasure. I never catch myself at any time without a perception, and can never observe anything but the perception.”

There is no self behind the perceptions. Only the perceptions themselves, a constant stream of sensations, thoughts, emotions, memories.

Hume called this the bundle theory of the self: the self is not a thing, it is a bundle of perceptions, held together by nothing more than memory and habit.

The “I” is a grammatical convenience, not a metaphysical entity.

The Ship of Theseus, Turned Inward

The ancient paradox: if you replace every plank of a ship, is it still the same ship?

Now turn this inward.

The atoms in your body replace themselves continuously. Every seven to ten years, most of your cells are new. The neurons in your brain rewire constantly, new synaptic connections formed, old ones pruned. Your beliefs, memories, values, personality, all of these have changed since childhood.

What exactly is the thing that persists?

You might say: memory. The continuous narrative thread.

But memories are reconstructive, not reproductive. Every time you remember something, you are not retrieving a stored file, you are rebuilding it from fragments, influenced by everything that has happened since.

Your memory of your childhood is not your childhood. It is a present-day reconstruction, wearing the costume of the past.

Parfit and What Matters in Survival

Derek Parfit’s Reasons and Persons (1984) is one of the most important philosophy books of the twentieth century, and one of the least read outside academic philosophy.

Parfit’s central question: what matters in survival?

He approached it through thought experiments.

Teletransportation: Suppose a machine scans every atom of your body, destroys the original, and recreates a perfect copy on Mars, same memories, same personality, same beliefs.

Is the person on Mars you?

Most people’s intuition: no. The original was destroyed. The Martian is a copy.

But Parfit asks: what if the machine malfunctions slightly, and doesn’t destroy the original? Now there are two of you, one on Earth, one on Mars. They are equally connected to your past self. Which one is you?

Neither can be, there can’t be two of you. But both have equal claim.

Parfit’s conclusion: personal identity is not what matters.

What matters is psychological continuity, the overlapping chains of memory, intention, belief, and character that connect your past self to your future self.

But these connections come in degrees. They can branch. They can fade. There is no sharp line where you begin and end.

The self is not a thing. It is a degree of connectedness.

And once you see this clearly, Parfit argued, it is deeply liberating.

The fear of death, properly understood, is the fear of the self’s dissolution. But if the self was never a unified, persistent thing to begin with, if it was always a process, always a matter of degree, then what exactly are you afraid of losing?

The Buddhist Diagnosis

Twenty-five centuries before Parfit, the Buddha arrived at the same conclusion.

The doctrine of anātman (Sanskrit) or anattā (Pāli): there is no permanent, unchanging self.

What we call the self is a collection of five aggregates (skandhas):

  1. Rūpa: form, the physical body
  2. Vedanā: sensation, feeling tone (pleasant/unpleasant/neutral)
  3. Saññā: perception, recognition
  4. Saṅkhāra: mental formations, volitions, habits
  5. Viññāṇa: consciousness, awareness

None of these is the self. The self is what arises when they interact, a process, not a substance.

The Buddha’s diagnosis: dukkha, suffering, dissatisfaction, arises from clinging to a self that was never there. We grasp at a fixed identity, resist change, build elaborate structures to protect an “I” that is more verb than noun.

The Buddhist path is not the annihilation of the self. It is the seeing through of the illusion, and the freedom that follows.

What is remarkable is that this is not mysticism. It is careful phenomenological analysis, arrived at through sustained introspective practice.

Hume would have recognized it immediately.

What Neuroscience Says

The neuroscientific picture is, if anything, more vertiginous.

The brain does not have a central processing unit, a “seat of the self” where everything comes together. Consciousness is not located anywhere in particular.

The default mode network (DMN), a set of brain regions active during self-referential thought, mind-wandering, and narrative construction, is sometimes called the “self network.” But it is a network, not a center. It is distributed, dynamic, constantly changing.

Benjamin Libet’s experiments (1983): subjects were asked to flex their wrist whenever they chose, and report the moment of conscious decision. The brain’s readiness potential, a measurable buildup of neural activity, preceded the reported moment of conscious decision by approximately 350 milliseconds.

The brain had already begun the movement before the subject decided to move.

If the conscious “I” did not initiate the action, if the decision was already underway before awareness of it, what role is the self playing?

Perhaps: narrator, not agent. The self may be a story the brain tells about itself, after the fact, to create the illusion of unified authorship.

You are not the driver. You are the passenger writing a real-time account of a journey that began before you picked up the pen.

The Paradox of the Introspecting Subject

Here is the deepest difficulty.

To investigate the self, you use the self. To question the “I,” an “I” does the questioning.

This is not merely circular, it is constitutively so. There is no view from nowhere. Every act of introspection is performed by the very thing under investigation.

Kant saw this and concluded the self, the transcendental unity of apperception, must be presupposed as the condition of all experience. You cannot step outside it. It is the frame, not the picture.

But the frame shapes what you see.

Living Without a Self

What are the practical consequences of taking this seriously?

Parfit wrote that when he fully absorbed the implications of his own view, his life changed:

“When I believed that my existence was such a further fact, I seemed imprisoned in myself. My life seemed like a glass tunnel, through which I was moving faster every year, and at the end of which there was darkness. When I changed my view, the walls of my glass tunnel disappeared. I now live in the open air.”

The dissolution of the self, not as a metaphysical claim but as a lived reality, is the goal of contemplative traditions from Buddhism to Stoicism to certain strands of Christian mysticism.

Marcus Aurelius:

“Things themselves touch not the soul, not in the least degree, nor have they admission to the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul; but the soul turns and moves itself alone.”

Epictetus:

“Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.”

These are not mere platitudes. They are practical consequences of a metaphysics, the Stoic view that the self is not identical to the body, the reputation, the career, the opinions of others. The self, properly understood, is rational agency. And rational agency cannot be taken from you.

Where This Leaves Us

Does the self exist?

The honest answer: not in the way you think it does.

There is experience. There is continuity of a kind. There is a perspective, a point of view.

But the unified, persistent, indivisible “I”, the Cartesian subject, the soul, the ghost in the machine, this does not survive scrutiny.

Hume didn’t find it. Parfit dissolved it. The Buddha saw through it. Neuroscience cannot locate it.

And yet, here you are, reading this, with the overwhelming sense that someone is reading.

Perhaps that sense is itself the answer. Not the self as substance, but the self as process. Not a noun, but a verb.

Not I am, but there is experiencing.

And maybe, just maybe, that is enough to go on with.

Further reading:

Derek Parfit. Reasons and Persons (1984).

David Hume. A Treatise of Human Nature (1739).

Thomas Metzinger. Being No One (2003).

Antonio Damasio. The Feeling of What Happens (1999).

Bhikkhu Bodhi. In the Buddha’s Words (2005).

item.title: What Is Time? Augustine, Heidegger, and the Physics of the Passing Moment
item.description:
Augustine of Hippo, in the year 397, wrote one of the most honest sentences in the history of philosophy:

“Quid est ergo tempus? Si nemo ex me quaerat, scio; si quaerenti explicare velim, nescio.”

“What then is time? If no one asks me, I know. If I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know.”

He wrote this in the Confessions, a book that is itself a meditation on time, on memory, on the self that persists through the passing of moments.

He is right.

You know what time is in the way you know how to breathe. Without thinking about it, without being able to explain it.

The moment you try to explain it, the thing dissolves.

The present: where is it? By the time you name it, it is gone.

The past: it no longer exists. The future: it does not yet exist.

And yet time is the most real thing there is.

More real than space. More intimate than thought.

You are inside it right now. You cannot get out. You cannot examine it from outside.

This is the problem of time.

I. Augustine. Time as the Soul’s Extension

Augustine’s analysis of time in Book XI of the Confessions is the first great philosophical account of temporal experience.

His starting point: the cosmological question.

“What was God doing before the Creation?”

The naive answer: preparing hell for those who ask such questions. :) (Ahahhahahha!)

Augustine quotes this with gentle irony.

His real answer: the question is malformed.

Before the Creation, there was no time. Time was created with the world. “Before” requires time. There is no before.

“Et nullum tempus, antequam faceres aliquid, fuit, quoniam et ipsum tempus tu fecisti.”

“And no time was, before you made anything, since you yourself made time.”

This is a profound move: time is not the container in which events occur. Time is itself created. It is part of the universe, not the stage on which the universe performs.

Both Augustine and Einstein refuse to treat time as a fixed container that exists independently of everything else. Augustine gets there through theology, Einstein through mathematics. The reasoning is completely different. But the destination has an odd resemblance.

(Whether this counts as anticipation or coincidence is a fair question. I lean toward interesting coincidence.)

The three presents:

Augustine’s most famous contribution to the philosophy of time:

The past does not exist. It is gone. The future does not exist. It has not yet come. The present is a knife-edge. It passes before you can name it.

And yet: we experience all three.

How?

Through the soul.

“Praesens de praeteritis memoria, praesens de praesentibus contuitus, praesens de futuris expectatio.”

“The present of past things is memory, the present of present things is sight, the present of future things is expectation.”

The three modes of time are three modes of the soul’s attention:

Memory: the past held in the present.

Attention: the present grasped in the present.

Expectation: the future anticipated in the present.

All three are present. All three are in the soul.

Time is not out there in the world. It is in here, in the mind that holds past and future in its present attention.

“In te, anime meus, tempora metior.”

“In you, my soul, I measure time.”

This is Augustine’s radical claim: time is psychological.

Not in the sense that it is unreal, but in the sense that temporal experience is constituted by the mind’s activity of holding past, present, and future together.

The distension of the soul:

Augustine uses the word distentio, distension, stretching, to describe the soul’s temporal structure.

The soul is stretched across time. Pulled toward the past by memory, pulled toward the future by expectation, held at the present by attention.

(I have felt this. The soul stretched between what was and what might be, unable to rest in what is. Augustine named it correctly.)

This stretching is not comfortable. It is the source of anxiety, of the restlessness that Augustine describes in the Confessions’ most famous line:

“Inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te.”

“Our heart is restless, until it rests in you.”

The restlessness is temporal. The soul stretched across past and future, unable to rest in the present, is the condition of temporal existence.

Rest, the Sabbath, eternity, is the release from distension.

II. Heidegger. Being-Toward-Death

Martin Heidegger’s Being and Time (1927) is the most ambitious philosophical work of the twentieth century.

It’s an attempt to ask, for the first time since the Greeks, the fundamental question:

What does it mean to be?

And his answer: to understand being, you must understand time.

Because being is temporal. Everything that is, is in time.

Heidegger’s fundamental concept: Dasein, being-there, the kind of being that we are.

Dasein is not a subject contemplating an object. It is not a mind inside a body. It is being-in-the-world, already thrown into a situation, already caring about things, already engaged before reflection begins.

Thrownness:

We did not choose to exist. We did not choose our time, our place, our language, our body.

We found ourselves thrown into a situation not of our choosing.

This is Geworfenheit, thrownness.

The facticity of existence: that I am here, now, this, without having chosen any of it.

The temporality of Dasein:

Dasein is always:

Coming from a past it did not choose (thrownness), moving toward a future it cannot avoid (projection), existing in a present shaped by both.

This is the temporal structure of human existence: ecstatic temporality, the “ek-stasis” (standing-outside) of existing always beyond the present moment, always relating to what was and what will be.

Being-toward-death:

Heidegger’s most radical claim:

Death is not an event that happens at the end. Death is a structure of existence. Now.

I am always being-toward-death, always living in the light of my finitude, always existing as the being for whom my existence is an issue.

This is what distinguishes Dasein from a stone or a tree: not consciousness, exactly, but the fact that my being matters to me, that I must take a stand on it, that I cannot be indifferent to whether I exist.

Authentic and inauthentic existence:

Most of the time, we flee from the awareness of finitude.

We lose ourselves in the das Man, the “they,” the anonymous public, doing what one does, thinking what one thinks, living as one lives.

This is inauthenticity, not moral failure, but the everyday flight from the anxiety of genuine selfhood.

(This is the most uncomfortable part of Heidegger for me. Because he is right. Most of what I do on any given day is what “one does.” The genuine choices are rarer than I like to think.)

Authentic existence: confronting death, owning your thrownness, choosing from the possibilities that are genuinely yours, not because they are chosen for you by the anonymous they.

Anxiety:

For Heidegger, the mood that reveals the true structure of existence is Angst, anxiety.

Not fear of a specific thing. Anxiety is anxiety about nothing. About existence itself. About the groundlessness of being. About the fact that I am here without justification or guarantee.

Anxiety strips away the comfortable securities of everyday life and reveals what is always already there: the finite, temporal, groundless structure of human existence.

This is not pathology. It is clarity.

“Der Tod ist die eigenste Möglichkeit des Daseins.”

“Death is the ownmost possibility of Dasein.”

III. The Physics of Time. What Science Says

Philosophy asks: what is time?

Physics answers, partially, strangely, in ways that deepen the mystery rather than resolve it.

Newton’s absolute time:

For Newton, time is absolute, true, and mathematical, flowing equably, without relation to anything external.

It is the background, the container, in which events occur.

The same time passes for everyone, everywhere. There is a universal now.

This is what common sense tells us.

It is wrong.

Special relativity. The relativity of simultaneity:

Einstein showed (1905): simultaneity is relative.

Two events simultaneous in one reference frame are not simultaneous in another.

There is no universal now. The “same moment” means nothing without specifying a reference frame.

Time dilation: moving clocks run slow.

A clock on a fast-moving spaceship ticks more slowly than a clock at rest.

Not as an illusion. Really!

The astronaut who travels at near-light-speed ages more slowly than the person who stays.

Time is not absolute. It is woven into spacetime, a four-dimensional manifold in which time and space are related by the Lorentz transformation.

General relativity. Time curves:

In the presence of mass and energy, spacetime curves. Time itself curves.

Gravitational time dilation: clocks run slower in stronger gravitational fields.

A clock at sea level ticks more slowly than a clock on a mountain. Not by much. But measurably.

GPS satellites must account for this.

Near a black hole: time slows toward the event horizon. At the horizon: time stops, from the perspective of a distant observer.

The block universe:

The most radical implication of relativity:

The block universe, or eternalism, holds that past, present, and future all equally exist.

In special relativity, different observers disagree about which events are simultaneous. There is no preferred “now” that carves the four-dimensional spacetime into past and future.

If there is no preferred now, if “now” is relative to the observer, then the distinction between “things that exist (present)” and “things that no longer exist (past)” is also observer-dependent.

This is not the only interpretation. Presentism holds that only the present is real. The growing block theory holds that the past and present exist but the future does not.

These are live debates in the philosophy of physics.

(I find the block universe unsettling but genuinely hard to argue against. Which is probably how it should feel.)

The arrow of time:

If the laws of physics are time-symmetric, if the equations of QM and GR look the same run forwards and backwards, why does time have a direction?

Why do we remember the past but not the future? Why do broken eggs not reassemble? Why does entropy increase?

The arrow of time is associated with entropy increase. But why entropy was low at the Big Bang, and why this produces our experience of time’s direction, remains genuinely open.

The universe began in an improbable, low-entropy configuration. Everything since has been moving toward greater disorder.

This is the direction we call “future.”

But the deeper question, why that initial condition, cannot be answered from within the physics.

The Planck time:

At \(t_P \approx 5.39 \times 10^{-44}\) seconds, the Planck time, our physics breaks down.

Before the Planck time after the Big Bang: the concept of time may not apply.

Quantum gravity, which we do not have, is needed to describe what “time” means at the Planck scale.

Whether time is continuous or discrete, whether it had a beginning, whether it will have an end, these are questions our physics cannot currently answer.

IV. The Experience of Time. Phenomenology

Between Augustine’s psychological time and physics’ geometrical time, there is a third perspective: the phenomenology of temporal experience.

Husserl’s time-consciousness:

Edmund Husserl, Heidegger’s teacher, analyzed the structure of the “living present” in On the Phenomenology of the Consciousness of Internal Time (1928).

The present moment, for Husserl, is not a knife-edge, an instantaneous now with no duration.

It is a specious present, a small stretch of time that is experienced as simultaneous.

Within this living present:

retention, the just-past, still held in the present experience, and protention, the about-to-come, already anticipated.

When you hear a melody, you hear the notes as a sequence, not as isolated sounds.

You hear them as a melody because the earlier notes are retained while the later notes are heard.

The present moment of hearing contains, within it, the retained past and the anticipated future.

This is why music is possible. This is why speech is possible.

Without retention and protention, each moment would be completely isolated, no connection to what came before, no anticipation of what comes next.

(This is why I cannot listen to music as background noise. The melody requires the whole present. You cannot half-hear it.)

Time-consciousness makes experience coherent.

The phenomenology of boredom:

Heidegger, in his 1929-30 lecture course The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics, analyzes boredom as a fundamental mood that reveals the structure of time.

When bored, time slows. Conspicuously.

You become aware of time’s passing precisely because it is not passing.

The structure revealed: time is normally transparent. We live through it without noticing it, absorbed in our activities.

Boredom makes time opaque, suddenly visible, heavy, resistant.

The bored person is held by time, unable to fill it, unable to move through it, exposed to its pure passing.

This is why boredom is so uncomfortable. It exposes the temporality of existence that absorption normally conceals.

The phenomenology of flow:

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi’s concept of flow, the state of complete absorption in a challenging activity, is the opposite of boredom.

In flow: time disappears. The person is entirely in the present, no past, no future, no awareness of duration.

Athletes, musicians, programmers, writers in the state of deep work, all report the disappearance of time.

Two hours pass in what feels like twenty minutes. Or twenty minutes feel like two hours.

The experience of time’s duration is not measured by the clock. It is constituted by the quality of attention.

Full attention: time disappears. Empty attention: time expands unbearably.

V. Memory. The Past That Lives

Augustine said: the present of past things is memory.

Memory is not a recording. It is a reconstruction.

The reconstructive nature of memory:

Every time you remember something, you reconstruct it, from fragments, from expectations, from your current emotional state, from the story you have been telling about your own past.

The remembered past is not the actual past. It is a present construction of what the past was.

This is not a failure of memory. It is what memory is.

The past, as experienced in memory, is always filtered through the present self doing the remembering.

Proust:

Marcel Proust spent 3,000 pages (I read them,yeah!) exploring this in In Search of Lost Time, the madeleine dipped in tea that suddenly releases a memory not as a record but as a full sensory re-experience, involuntary memory, the past that comes unbidden, more vivid than voluntary recollection, and the narrator’s realization that what he was searching for, lost time, could only be recovered in art, which makes the past permanent by making it the present of the reader. (Wooohoooo, this is Filiz’s longest sentence, a revenge of time spent reading Proust! :))

“The true paradises are the paradises we have lost.”

(3,000 pages on this one idea. And every page earns its place. This is either the most self-indulgent novel ever written or the most honest one. Probably both.)

The physics of memory:

Memory is encoded in synaptic connections, in the physical structure of the brain.

When you remember, neurons fire in patterns that recreate the original pattern.

But: each time you remember, the memory is slightly altered, reconsolidated with new information.

The memory of a memory is not the original experience. It is the memory of the last time you remembered it.

(Which means the memories I am most certain of are probably the most altered. Comforting thought.)

The past, neurologically, is continuously rewritten in the present.

VI. The Future. Expectation and Anxiety

Augustine: the present of future things is expectation.

The future does not exist. And yet we live oriented toward it.

Every action is directed toward a future state. Every plan assumes a future. Every hope, every fear, every intention, all are directed toward what is not yet.

Heidegger’s Entwurf, projection, the way Dasein always throws itself ahead toward possibilities.

We are not beings who have a future. We are beings who are always already projecting ourselves toward a future, who exist in the mode of the not-yet.

The tyranny of the future:

The future that concerns us most is the one we cannot plan for: death.

The awareness of mortality, explicit or implicit, shapes the entire temporal horizon of experience.

Everything is done in the light of finitude.

Every choice involves the other choices that are thereby not made.

Every moment contains the mortality that makes it this moment and not an infinite succession of others.

This is not morbidity. It is the condition of seriousness.

The person who genuinely lives in the awareness of finitude takes their time seriously, knows that this moment is not replaceable, that this conversation, this decision, this experience, will not come again.

The person who lives in denial of finitude can always defer. There will be time later, another chance, a tomorrow that is structurally identical to today.

Death cancels the infinite deferral. It makes the present the only time there is.

VII. The Eternal Present

Against the rushing of time, the Buddhist, the Stoic, the contemplative traditions of many cultures have proposed a different relationship with time:

The eternal present.

Not eternity as infinite duration, time going on forever.

But eternity as the depth of the present, the present moment experienced in its fullness, without the pull of past or future.

Marcus Aurelius:

“Confine yourself to the present.”

Not as a counsel of forgetfulness, but as a recognition that the past and future are not available to us. Only the present is real. Only the present can be inhabited.

The mind that is always elsewhere, in the regretted past, in the anxious future, is never where it is.

The physics of the present:

In special relativity, the light cone of an event divides spacetime into three regions: the past (what could have caused this event), the future (what this event could cause), and the spacelike-separated region, a vast set of events that cannot be causally connected to this event at all.

The “absolute present” in this sense is not a thin slice. It is enormous.

The contemplative idea of a deep, full present is philosophically interesting. But it does not map onto the physics in any tidy way.

The poetry is tempting. The physics does not cooperate.

VIII. Time and Language

Wittgenstein noted: the grammar of our language generates philosophical puzzles about time.

“Time passes,” but what is the subject? What is doing the passing?

“The same moment,” what makes moments the same or different?

“Now,” the most indexical word in language, pointing to the present, cannot be given a description that is not itself indexical.

Every attempt to describe “now” uses another word that refers to now.

The grammar of temporal language is not a description of time. It is a form of life, a set of practices for coordinating human activity in time.

When we ask “what is time?” we may be asking: what is the grammar of temporal language?

And the answer may be: there is no deeper answer. The grammar is what it is. The practices are what they are.

Time is what we do with it!

IX. What We Don’t Know

After Augustine, after Heidegger, after Einstein, after quantum mechanics, what do we know about time?

We know:

Time dilates with velocity and gravity.

The arrow of time is associated with entropy increase, though why entropy was low at the Big Bang remains unexplained.

Time had a beginning, the Big Bang.

Below the Planck time, time has no meaning.

We don’t know:

Whether time flows or is static.

Whether the present is real or relative.

Whether time is continuous or discrete.

Whether time had a beginning in any absolute sense.

What happened before the Big Bang, or whether “before” applies.

Why the universe began in a low-entropy state, which is the real origin of the arrow of time.

Whether time is fundamental or emergent.

The deepest mystery:

Why does time seem to flow?

In the block universe, all moments equally exist. Nothing moves. Nothing passes. The universe is a static four-dimensional structure.

And yet: you experience time as flowing.

The present feels different from the past. The future feels open in a way the past does not.

Why?

This question, the question of why we experience time as flowing in a world where physics suggests nothing flows, is the hardest question in the philosophy of time.

It connects physics to consciousness. It connects the structure of the world to the structure of experience.

It has no agreed answer.

X. Living in Time

All of this philosophy, all of this physics, and time remains what it was before any of it:

The medium of your life. The stuff you are made of. The dimension in which everything happens, everything you remember, everything you anticipate, everything you are doing right now.

Augustine’s restless heart. Heidegger’s being-toward-death. Einstein’s dilating clocks. Proust’s involuntary memory. The Stoic’s present moment.

All of these are attempts to understand the same thing:

What it is to be a being who exists in time, who is constituted by past, oriented toward future, and always already in the present that passes before it can be held.

The answer is not available. The question is indispensable.

“Si nemo ex me quaerat, scio.”

If no one asks me, I know.

I know it right now, this moment, this passing, this movement from what was to what will be through the knife-edge of what is.

I know it in the way I know how to breathe.

And when I try to explain it, I do not know.

Further reading:

Augustine. Confessions (397). (trans. Henry Chadwick, Oxford World’s Classics). Book XI for the philosophy of time.

Heidegger. Being and Time (1927). (trans. Macquarrie & Robinson, or Stambaugh). Division Two for temporality and death.

Husserl. On the Phenomenology of the Consciousness of Internal Time (1928). (trans. Brough, Kluwer).

McTaggart. “The Unreality of Time” (1908). Mind 17, 457. The A-series / B-series distinction; essential.

Price. Time’s Arrow and Archimedes’ Point (1996). Oxford University Press.

Barbour. The End of Time (1999). Oxford University Press.

Rovelli. The Order of Time (2018).

Proust. In Search of Lost Time :)) (Filizko suffered, now it is your turn! Ahahah!) :)) (trans. Moncrieff & Kilmartin).

Penrose. The Road to Reality (2004). Chapters 27-28 for time asymmetry.

item.title: Is Life Worth Living? Camus, Seneca, and the Only Question That Matters
item.description:
My first attempt to read The Myth of Sisyphus was at 26.

Camus opens the book with:

“There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.”

I put it down after the first sentence. Not because it was difficult. Because I was afraid of it.

I had lost my professor, Ritchie Eanes, to suicide at 22. He was someone I loved very much. I thought I had healed. The first sentence felt like something pulling at a scar I didn’t want opened.

There was also my grandmother’s faith, which I had grown up inside: the belief that suicide is the gravest sin. Even in Go, the game I play, it is a forbidden move. The book seemed to be building a justification for something I did not want justified. I walked away.

I came back at 35!

By then I had buried my grandmother. I had stood at her grave, then I turned around, and walked back to my life.

We had both died that day. And, they only buried her.

Something happens when you lose the person you love most. The things that used to frighten you stop frightening you. Most people are afraid of cemeteries at night. If cemeteries still scare you, you probably haven’t lost that person yet.

I am not afraid of cemeteries anymore. Not even at night. The word “suicide” doesn’t frighten me either. I knew why I was living.

So, Camus again. At 35.

“There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.”

This time I understood: it is not an invitation. It is a test. If you don’t know why you keep living, you are not really living. You are drifting.

Are you drifting?

“There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.”

This is not provocation for its own sake. It is a precise philosophical claim, and understanding what Camus means by it requires reading the sentence carefully.

He is not asking whether you should die. He is asking whether you have answered the prior question: why you should live.

If you have not answered that question, if you are simply continuing by inertia, by habit, by the absence of a decisive reason to stop, then Camus’s claim is that you have not yet begun to philosophize in any serious sense.

You are deferring the question.

Philosophy, for Camus, begins at the moment you stop deferring it.

I. The Absurd, Precisely Defined

Camus is often misread as a nihilist. He is the opposite.

The nihilist says: there is no meaning. Camus says: the question of meaning is the most urgent question there is, which is exactly the opposite of nihilism.

The absurd is not meaninglessness.

It is a relation, a confrontation between two things:

  1. The human demand for clarity, meaning, unity, the need to understand, to find coherence, to have the world answer back when you question it.

  2. The world’s silence, its total indifference to that demand.

“The absurd is born of the confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world.”

Neither term alone produces the absurd. A human being without the need for meaning: no absurd. A silent world with no one demanding answers: no absurd.

The absurd requires both, the demand and the silence, in permanent, irresolvable confrontation.

The absurd is not a conclusion. It is a starting point.

Once you have recognized the absurd, once you have seen that the world will not give you what you are asking for, the question is: what do you do with that recognition?

Camus identifies three possible responses:

1. Physical suicide: Eliminate the human term of the equation. No more human demand, no more absurd.

Camus rejects this. It is not a solution. It is an evasion. It destroys the consciousness that recognized the absurd rather than confronting the recognition.

2. Philosophical suicide: Leap to faith, to God, to transcendence, to any system that claims to resolve the tension by providing meaning from outside.

Camus rejects this too, more forcefully. It is intellectual dishonesty: the recognition of the absurd is real, and papering over it with faith does not make it less real. It makes you less honest.

3. Revolt: Accept the absurd. Refuse to resolve it. Live inside the tension, in full awareness of the silence, without flinching, without leaping.

This is Camus’s answer.

II. Sisyphus, The Argument in Image

Camus takes the myth of Sisyphus and reads it as the image of the human condition.

Sisyphus was condemned by the gods to push a boulder up a hill for eternity. Each time he reaches the top, the boulder rolls back down. He descends. He pushes again. Forever.

The traditional reading: this is punishment. The futility is the horror.

Camus’s reading: Sisyphus is the absurd hero.

He knows what he is doing. He knows the boulder will roll back. He knows the task will never be completed. He pushes anyway.

The gods thought they were punishing him with futility. But Sisyphus, in full consciousness of his condition, has taken ownership of it.

The futility belongs to the gods’ design. The act of pushing belongs to Sisyphus.

“One must imagine Sisyphus happy.”

This is the most famous line in the essay, and the most misunderstood.

Camus is not saying Sisyphus is cheerful. He is not saying the suffering is not real. He is saying:

Happiness, for Camus, is not the absence of suffering or the presence of meaning.

It is the condition of the person who has faced the absurd fully, who knows exactly what their situation is, and who chooses to continue in full awareness of that situation.

The happiness is in the lucidity, not in the outcome.

I came to this book expecting not to believe it. Camus convinced me anyway.

The descent:

Camus focuses particularly on the moment when Sisyphus descends from the top of the hill back to the boulder.

During the ascent: effort, engagement, the task. During the descent: consciousness.

“I leave Sisyphus at the foot of the mountain! One always finds one’s burden again. But Sisyphus teaches the higher fidelity that negates the gods and raises rocks. He too considers things to be good. This universe henceforth without a master seems to him neither sterile nor futile. Each atom of that stone, each mineral flake of that night-filled mountain, in itself forms a world. The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart.”

The descent is the moment of freedom, the moment between the futility of the top and the resumption of the task.

In that moment, Sisyphus is free. Not from his condition. From the need for his condition to be otherwise.

III. Seneca, The Urgency of Time

Lucius Annaeus Seneca wrote his Letters to Lucilius around 65 CE, in the last years of his life, under Nero, aware that death could come at any moment by imperial order.

It did come. Nero ordered him to die. He opened his veins.

The Letters are the work of a man who has thought seriously about mortality and decided to write it down before it was too late.

The most important sentence:

“Omnia, Lucili, aliena sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est.”

“Everything, Lucilius, belongs to others; time alone is ours.”

When I first read this, my reaction was: really? Is that all we have?

And then: yes. That is all we have.

The accountability this requires is terrifying. To really accept it, you have to admit how much time you have already given away, and to what.

I think most people cannot open their arms to a truth this deep. We prefer the surface. It is more comfortable there. The bacteria find their ideal conditions at the surface of things, and so, mostly, do we.

Absurdism lives exactly here: in the gap between the depth of the question and our preference for staying shallow.

This is not a casual observation. It is the conclusion of a sustained argument about the nature of loss and possession.

Your property can be taken. Your reputation can be destroyed. Your relationships can be ended. Your health can be lost. Your status can be stripped.

All of these are held conditionally, on loan from fortune, which gives and takes without explanation.

Time is different.

Or rather: time should be different. Because most people treat time as the most expendable of their possessions, giving it away freely, wasting it without regret, allowing others to consume it without resistance.

“Ita fac, mi Lucili: vindica te tibi.”

“Do this, my Lucilius: claim yourself for yourself.”

Seneca is not asking you to become selfish. He is asking you to treat your time with at least the care you give to your money, to notice when it is being taken, to choose deliberately what you give it to, to not hand it over by default.

The accounting of time:

Seneca returns obsessively to the image of accounting, of calculating what you have, what you have spent, what remains.

“Persuade tibi hoc sic esse ut scribo: quaedam tempora eripiuntur nobis, quaedam subducuntur, quaedam effluunt.”

“Convince yourself that this is true: some moments are snatched from us, some are stolen, and some slip away.”

Not the days you were alive. The days that were genuinely yours, spent on what you chose, in the presence of what mattered, doing what you intended to do.

The rest: given away. To other people’s demands. To obligations you did not choose. To the noise that fills the space between one genuine moment and the next.

“Nusquam est qui ubique est.”

“One who is everywhere is nowhere.”

The person who is always available, always responsive, always accommodating, who has no center of gravity, no place they have chosen to be, is, in Seneca’s analysis, not fully living.

Life, for Seneca, requires the capacity to say no, to refuse the infinite demands of other people’s time in order to protect something that is genuinely yours.

IV. The Same Question, Two Directions

Camus and Seneca are separated by nineteen centuries. They are asking the same question.

Camus asks: given that the world is silent, why continue?

Seneca asks: given that time is finite, what are you doing with it?

Both questions assume that the default, continuation without reflection, life lived by inertia, is not sufficient.

Both demand that you become the conscious author of your own existence rather than its passive passenger.

Neither offers consolation in the conventional sense.

Camus does not say the world will become meaningful. He says: live in full awareness of the fact that it won’t.

Seneca does not say you will have enough time. He says: the time you have is enough if you stop wasting it.

Both locate the solution not in changing the external conditions, the world’s silence, the finitude of time, but in changing the relationship between the self and those conditions.

The world stays silent. The time stays finite. What changes: you.

Camus is interested in the moment, the present confrontation with the absurd, the descent of Sisyphus, the atom of time in which consciousness recognizes its situation and chooses revolt.

Seneca is interested in the span, the whole of a life, viewed as a quantity to be managed, a resource to be allocated with the seriousness it deserves.

Camus asks: are you alive right now?

Seneca asks: have you been alive across the whole of your time?

They are not contradictory questions. They are the microscope and the telescope aimed at the same object.

V. The Absurd and Time, Together

Read together, Camus and Seneca produce a complete philosophical position.

The world will not give you meaning. This is Camus’s premise. Accept it. Stop waiting for the silence to break.

Your time is the only thing you have. This is Seneca’s premise. Take it seriously. Stop giving it away by default.

The synthesis:

If the world is silent, if meaning is not given but made, then the only raw material you have for making it is time.

Your time, spent on what you chose, in full awareness of the silence, without the consolation of an answer that was never coming, this is what a life is.

Not the achievement of meaning. The construction of it, moment by moment, from the only material available: the hours that are genuinely yours.

Sisyphus with his hours:

Return to Sisyphus.

The boulder is the task, whatever task you have chosen or been given. The hill is time, finite, steep. The descent is the moment of consciousness.

But Seneca adds something Camus does not:

The question of what Sisyphus does with the hours that are not pushing.

The descent, yes. But also: the time at the foot of the mountain before he begins again.

Does he give that time away? Does he let it be consumed by other people’s demands, by noise, by the refusal to be present?

Or does he claim it?

Vindica te tibi.

Claim yourself for yourself.

Even Sisyphus, condemned to eternal futility, has hours. What he does with them, whether he inhabits them or squanders them, is the only freedom he has.

It is the only freedom any of us has.

VI. The Only Serious Question, Revisited

Camus said there is only one serious philosophical question.

He meant: before you can do any other philosophy, before ethics, epistemology, metaphysics, you must answer this.

Because if you have not answered it, if you are continuing by default, by inertia, by the absence of a reason to stop, then your philosophy is built on nothing.

Seneca’s version of the same demand:

“Ita fac, mi Lucili: vindica te tibi.”

Before you can give your time to anything, you must first claim it as yours.

Both philosophers are making the same foundational demand:

Wake up.

Not in the motivational sense. In the philosophical sense.

Become the conscious author of your own existence. Stop deferring the question.

The question is: is this life, this specific life, lived in this specific way, worth living?

Not life in general. Not life in principle. This life. As you are living it. Right now.

If the answer is yes: you know why. You have examined it. You are not drifting.

If the answer is no: you know what needs to change. Not whether to continue, but what continuing should mean.

If you have not asked the question: Camus and Seneca, nineteen centuries apart, are both waiting.

“There is but one truly serious philosophical question.”

“Everything belongs to others; time alone is ours.”

Same question. Same urgency. Different words.

Further reading:

Camus. The Myth of Sisyphus (1942). (trans. Justin O’Brien, Vintage). Read the full essay, not just the famous lines.

Seneca. Letters to Lucilius (c. 65 CE). (trans. Robin Campbell, Penguin Classics). Letters I, III, and LXXVII especially.

Seneca. On the Shortness of Life. (trans. C.D.N. Costa, Penguin Classics).

Matthew Sharpe. Camus, Philosophe (2015).

Miriam Griffin. Seneca: A Philosopher in Politics (1976).

item.title: Seneca: On Time, Death, and the Art of Living Before You Die
item.description:
“Omnia, Lucili, aliena sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est.”

Everything, Lucilius, belongs to others. Time alone is ours.

Seneca wrote this in a letter. He was an old man.

He had been one of the most powerful men in Rome, tutor and advisor to Nero, the most feared emperor in history.

He had been extraordinarily wealthy. He had been exiled, recalled, celebrated, suspected.

And he sat down and wrote to his friend Lucilius: time alone is ours.

Not the palace. Not the money. Not the influence. Not the books or the reputation or the name.

Time.

And then, immediately, the continuation:

“In huius rei unius fugacis ac lubricae possessionem natura nos misit, ex qua expellit quicumque vult.”

Nature has put us in possession of only this one fleeting and slippery thing, from which anyone who wishes can drive us out.

I. The Man

Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born around 4 BCE in Córdoba, in Roman Spain.

He came to Rome as a child, studied rhetoric and philosophy, became a brilliant advocate and writer, and rose to prominence under the emperor Claudius.

Then Claudius’s wife accused him of adultery with the emperor’s niece. He was exiled to Corsica for eight years.

He was recalled by Agrippina, Claudius’s new wife, Nero’s mother, to serve as tutor to her son.

When Nero became emperor at sixteen, Seneca was his most important advisor.

For several years, the partnership worked, Seneca’s moderation restraining the emperor’s cruelty.

Then it didn’t.

Nero became what Nero became.

Seneca retreated from public life, tried to give back his wealth, tried to disengage from the court.

In 65 CE, Nero accused him of involvement in the Pisonian conspiracy, a plot to assassinate the emperor. The evidence was thin. It didn’t matter.

Nero sent soldiers to Seneca’s villa with an order to die.

Seneca opened his veins.

He died slowly. The veins of an old man do not bleed quickly.

He took poison; it didn’t work. He was placed in a hot bath to hasten the bleeding.

He dictated to scribes until he could no longer speak.

He died as he had written, discussing philosophy in the face of death, practicing what he had preached in letter after letter, essay after essay, for thirty years.

II. On the Shortness of Life

De Brevitate Vitae, On the Shortness of Life, is perhaps the most important thing Seneca wrote.

It begins with a paradox:

“It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a great deal of it.”

Life is not short. Life is long enough, more than long enough, if used well.

The problem is not the quantity of time. It is what we do with it.

We give our time to everyone who asks. We guard our money carefully. We are appalled if someone wastes our property. But we let people waste our hours, our days, our years, without protest, without even noticing.

“People are frugal in guarding their personal property; but as soon as it comes to squandering time they are most wasteful of the one thing in which it is right to be stingy.”

Seneca identifies the thieves of time:

The ambitious. Always preparing to live, always arranging the conditions under which life will begin. First I need this promotion. Then this house. Then this security. Then I will begin to live.

The pleasure-seekers. Always consuming, never present, always moving to the next experience.

The distracted. Pulled in every direction by other people’s urgencies, never attending to their own.

The greedy. Spending their life accumulating what life cannot be lived without spending.

All of them, Seneca says, are dying badly. Not because death is near but because they are not living.

“They lose the day in expectation of the night, and the night in fear of the dawn.”

III. The Letters to Lucilius

The Epistulae Morales, Moral Letters to Lucilius, are Seneca’s masterpiece.

One hundred and twenty-four letters, written in the last years of his life, to his friend Gaius Lucilius Junior, a man younger than Seneca, a government official in Sicily, who had apparently asked Seneca to help him live better.

The letters are not treatises. They are not systematic philosophy.

They are the most intimate philosophical document from the ancient world, a man thinking out loud, revising himself, admitting uncertainty, sharing what he has learned and what he has failed to learn.

They begin, famously:

“Ita fac, mi Lucili: vindica te tibi.”

Do this, my Lucilius: claim yourself for yourself.

The first letter. The first sentence. Already everything is there.

Claim yourself for yourself. Take back the time that has been dispersed, the attention that has been scattered, the self that has been given away in small pieces to everyone who asked.

Each letter takes up a theme: friendship, travel, the fear of death, anger, grief, luxury, poverty, solitude, crowds.

And works it through with a combination of personal reflection, philosophical argument, and the occasional devastating aphorism that lodges in the memory and will not leave.

IV. On Friendship

Seneca’s letters are, above all, about friendship.

Not friendship as a social category, as acquaintance, as usefulness, as pleasant company.

Friendship as the deepest form of human connection, the relationship in which another person is genuinely known and genuinely valued.

“Hoc primum philosophia promittit: sensum communem, humanitatem et congregationem.”

“Philosophy promises above all: common sense, humanity, and fellowship.”

And more directly:

“Sine amico nemo tutus vivere potest.”

“Without a friend, no one can live securely.”

But Seneca is precise about what friendship requires:

“Before you make a friend, judge whether he is worthy to be made a friend. After you have made a friend, trust him with everything.”

The order matters. Judgment first. Then total trust.

There is no friendship without judgment, the assessment of character, of values, of reliability.

And there is no friendship with only judgment. The trust must be complete, or it is not friendship.

He also says something that feels almost modern in its psychological precision:

“Recede in te ipse quantum potes.”

“Retire into yourself as much as you can.”

Solitude and friendship are not opposites for Seneca. They are complementary disciplines.

You must know yourself before you can truly know another. And you must know another to truly know yourself.

The friend is a mirror. Not a flattering one, but an honest one.

“Refer everything to a good person who you would want to imitate. Live as if he is watching.”

V. On Death

Seneca returns to death in almost every letter.

Not morbidly, not with the fascination of depression, but with the insistence of a man who has understood that the refusal to think about death is the primary source of the wasted life.

“Omnia, Lucili, aliena sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est.”

Time is ours, and it runs out.

To not know this, to live as if you will not die, is to be unable to choose.

You cannot choose well what to do with your life if you do not know how much of it remains.

You cannot prioritize correctly if you believe there will always be more time.

“Cogita quantum temporis absumpserit.”

“Think how much time has already been consumed.”

Not to produce guilt. To produce clarity.

The Stoic exercise of memento mori, remember that you will die, is not pessimism.

It is the most practical philosophical tool Seneca describes: the practice of holding death in mind as the clarifying horizon against which all choices become legible.

What matters, if today were the last day? What would you stop doing? What would you start?

“Dum differtur vita transcurrit.”

“While we are postponing, life speeds by.”

And his most personal formulation, written, perhaps, when the soldiers were already on their way:

“Omnia, Lucili, aliena sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est. In hoc unum avarus esse licet.”

“Everything belongs to others, Lucilius; time alone is ours. In this one thing it is permitted to be a miser.”

Be a miser with time. Give it to no one carelessly. Spend it on nothing that does not deserve it.

VI. The Stoic Framework

Seneca was a Stoic, part of the philosophical school founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens around 300 BCE.

But he was an unusual Stoic, the most human of them, the most willing to admit difficulty, the most honest about the gap between what philosophy teaches and what a person actually does.

The Stoic framework:

The dichotomy of control. Some things are up to us: our judgments, desires, aversions. Some things are not: our body, reputation, wealth, other people.

Unhappiness comes from wanting what is not up to us. Freedom comes from wanting only what is up to us.

The discipline of desire. Desire only what virtue requires. Prefer, but do not require: health, wealth, friendship. Be indifferent, in the technical sense, to everything external.

Living according to nature. The rational animal’s nature is reason. To live well is to live rationally, in accordance with the logos, the rational principle that structures reality.

Seneca accepted all of this. He also accepted that he often failed to live it.

This honesty is what distinguishes him from the more austere Stoics: Epictetus, who was enslaved and never complained, Marcus Aurelius, who ruled an empire and wrote his private doubts in a notebook.

Seneca was wealthy, powerful, sometimes hypocritical. He wrote about the dangers of wealth while being extraordinarily rich. He wrote about the importance of not fearing death while apparently fearing it.

His critics, then and now, point this out.

His response, in one of the letters:

“I am not a wise man, nor shall I ever be one. Demand of me not that I be equal to the best, but that I be better than the wicked. I am satisfied if I subtract something from my vices each day.”

Not perfection. Improvement.

Not the ideal Stoic sage, a figure even the Stoics admitted was theoretical.

A man trying, imperfectly, daily, to do better.

This is what makes him readable across two thousand years.

VII. The Consolations

Seneca wrote three formal consolations, letters to people in grief, that are among the most moving prose of the ancient world.

To Marcia: a woman who had lost her son. To Helvia: his own mother, written during his exile. To Polybius: a freedman at Claudius’s court, who had lost his brother.

The Ad Helviam, to his mother, is extraordinary.

He has been exiled. He is in Corsica, far from Rome, far from his work, far from his friends.

And he writes to his mother not to receive consolation but to give it.

“I have decided, dearest mother, to conquer my grief rather than to cheat it.”

He does not pretend the exile doesn’t hurt. He does not perform Stoic indifference.

He acknowledges the pain, his pain, her pain, and then works, carefully, philosophically, to find the resources within that pain for endurance.

The resources he finds:

the constancy of virtue, which cannot be exiled.

The life of the mind, which no location can confine.

The friendship of philosophy, which travels everywhere.

The love between mother and son, which distance cannot touch.

“Wherever I turn, I see the proofs of your affection.”

This is Stoicism with a human face. Not the denial of feeling but its transformation through honest philosophical attention.

VIII. Seneca and Power

The most difficult question about Seneca is the one his critics have always asked:

How do you square the philosophy with the life?

He wrote about the dangers of wealth, and was fabulously wealthy.

He wrote about the importance of virtue, and served a murderer.

He wrote about the shortness of life, and spent much of it in the service of Nero’s court.

Did he know what Nero was? Almost certainly.

Did he stay because he believed he could moderate the evil? Perhaps. For a time.

Did he stay too long? Almost certainly.

The charge of hypocrisy is serious. Philosophy that cannot be lived is not philosophy. It is literature.

Seneca’s answer, from the letters:

“Do not look at who says this, look at what is said.”

The teaching stands independent of the teacher. The truth of omnia aliena sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est does not depend on whether Seneca spent his own time well.

This is both a defense and an evasion. It is also, in a certain limited sense, right.

The letters are true whether Seneca lived them or not. But they would be truer if he had.

And we should hold both truths together, the wisdom of the letters and the failure of the life, without letting either cancel the other.

This is what it means to read a philosopher honestly.

IX. The Death

When the soldiers came, Seneca was ready.

Or as ready as a man can be who has spent decades preparing and still, in the end, is a body that bleeds slowly.

He tried to comfort his wife, Paulina, who wanted to die with him. He asked her to live.

“I showed you ways of looking after life; you prefer the glory of dying. I will not begrudge you such a noble example. Let the fortitude of this our common end be alike, but let there be more in your departure that is worthy of praise.”

She survived. Nero ordered it. She lived many years after.

The scars on her wrists marked her for the rest of her life.

Seneca dictated his last words. We do not know exactly what they were. Tacitus says they were spoken to friends and scribes. But he died speaking.

Still thinking. Still in the letters.

X. What He Gives Us

Seneca gives us something that most philosophers do not:

The permission to be imperfect while still trying.

Not the Platonic philosopher-king who has seen the sun. Not the Zen master who has achieved emptiness. Not the perfect Stoic sage who is indifferent to everything external.

A man. Brilliant, flawed, compromised, trying.

Writing letters to a friend about how to live better.

“Nusquam est qui ubique est.”

“One who is everywhere is nowhere.”

“Recede in te ipse quantum potes.”

“Retire into yourself as much as you can.”

“Ita fac, mi Lucili: vindica te tibi.”

“Claim yourself for yourself.”

Two thousand years old. Written this morning. Written for you. :)

Further reading:

Seneca. Letters from a Stoic (trans. Robin Campbell, Penguin Classics).

Seneca. On the Shortness of Life (trans. C.D.N. Costa).

Seneca. Dialogues and Essays (trans. John Davie, Oxford World’s Classics).

For context: Paul Veyne. Seneca: The Life of a Stoic (2003).

For the Stoic framework: Marcus Aurelius. Meditations (trans. Gregory Hays).
