item.title: Camus's The Stranger: On Indifference, Honesty, and the Unbearable Lightness of Not Pretending
item.description:
“Maman died today. Or yesterday maybe, I don’t know.”

This is the most famous opening sentence in twentieth century literature.

In French: “Aujourd’hui, maman est morte. Ou peut-être hier, je ne sais pas.”

Eight words in French. A mother is dead. The narrator is not sure when. He does not seem particularly troubled by his uncertainty.

Every reader who has ever opened this novel has felt, in these two sentences, something that is difficult to name: discomfort, provocation, recognition, unease.

The question the novel poses immediately, before anything else: what is wrong with this man?

The question it takes two parts and 123 pages to answer: nothing. And everything. And the everything is us, not him.

I. Camus and the Novel He Wrote at Twenty-Seven

Albert Camus published L’Étranger in 1942.

He was twenty-eight years old. France was under German occupation. Sartre reviewed it in Cahiers du Sud and called it one of the best works of the French literary renaissance.

Camus was born in Algeria in 1913, the son of a French Algerian father who died in World War I before Camus was two years old, and a partially deaf, nearly illiterate Spanish mother who cleaned houses to support her children.

He grew up in poverty in Algiers, in a small apartment with no books, no electricity, a grandmother who beat him with a whip made from bull’s hide, and a mother who sat in silence by the window in the evenings, lost in a world her disability made increasingly inaccessible.

His mother is everywhere in his work. She is in the silence. In the distance. In the particular quality of presence-without-communication that runs through everything Camus wrote.

And she is, unmistakably, in the dead maman of The Stranger’s first sentence. Not because Camus’s mother was dead (she outlived him) but because the relationship between Meursault and his mother encodes something Camus understood from childhood: that love and emotional expression are not the same thing, that the absence of performance is not the absence of feeling, that the world will punish you for failing to perform what it cannot verify you feel.

II. Meursault, The Man Who Will Not Lie

Meursault is not a psychopath.

This is the most common misreading of the novel, encouraged, it must be said, by Camus’s own early description of the character as a man “in love with truth”, and it is wrong in a way that matters.

A psychopath lacks affect, lacks genuine emotional response.

Meursault has affect. He feels pleasure (swimming, sex, the sun), discomfort (heat, social obligation, the interrogation), and something that may be a form of love, or may be the closest he can come to it, for his mother, for Marie, for Raymond in his way.

What Meursault lacks is not feeling. What he lacks is the willingness, or the ability, to perform feeling he does not currently have.

At his mother’s vigil, he does not weep. Not because he did not love her, the novel gives us no evidence he didn’t, but because he does not weep. The weeping is not there. He will not manufacture it.

He drinks café au lait at the vigil because he is tired and the coffee is offered. He smokes because he smokes.

He refuses the priest at the end because he does not believe, and he will not pretend to believe to make the priest more comfortable, even facing execution.

This is Meursault’s defining characteristic, not indifference, but radical honesty about his present state.

He will not say he is sad when he is not currently sad. He will not say he regrets when he does not currently feel regret. He will not say he believes when he does not believe.

He is constitutionally incapable of social performance.

III. The Sun and the Body

The novel’s first part is a masterpiece of sensory precision.

Camus writes Meursault’s experience almost entirely through physical sensation: heat, light, the smell of the sea, the weight of Marie against him in the water, the specific quality of Sunday afternoon emptiness.

This is not stylistic decoration. It is the novel’s central philosophical move.

Meursault lives in the body, in the immediate present, in sensation.

He does not narrate his life. He inhabits it. He does not interpret his experience. He reports it.

The style enacts the philosophy. Camus uses a stripped, declarative prose: short sentences, parataxis, the passé composé (the tense of completed, disconnected actions) rather than the imparfait (the tense of duration, background, continuity).

“I swam. Marie laughed. The water was cold. I helped her onto the float. We lay in the sun.”

No causality. No reflection. No narrative connection between events beyond their sequence in time.

This is not a character without an inner life. This is a character whose inner life is not primarily verbal or reflective. It is physical, immediate, present.

And then the sun.

The killing of the Arab on the beach is one of the most analyzed scenes in modern literature, and the analysis usually focuses on its apparent arbitrariness.

Meursault pulls the trigger because of the sun. Because the heat is unbearable, because the light off the Arab’s knife blinds him, because his body, pushed beyond its tolerance, acts before his mind can intervene.

“The trigger gave. I felt the smooth underside of the butt, and it was there, in that sharp but deafening noise, that it all started. I shook off the sweat and sun. I knew that I had shattered the harmony of the day, the exceptional silence of a beach where I’d been happy.”

Notice: he has shattered the harmony of the day. Not ended a life, though he has done that too. The register is aesthetic, sensory, immediate.

This is not moral obtuseness. It is the novel’s most radical move: presenting a morally catastrophic act through the phenomenology of the person committing it, without ironic distance, without authorial condemnation, and trusting the reader to hold both registers at once.

IV. The Trial, Society’s Theater

The second part of the novel is a different kind of masterpiece.

Meursault is tried, ostensibly for murder. Actually for something else entirely.

The prosecution builds its case not on the killing but on Meursault’s behavior at his mother’s funeral.

He did not weep. He drank coffee. He smoked.

He returned to Algiers the next day and went to the beach and slept with a woman and laughed at a Fernandel film.

This is the crime the court actually cares about.

The killing of the Arab is, in the novel’s moral economy, almost incidental, a pretext.

What the court cannot forgive, cannot absorb, cannot categorize safely, is a man who does not perform grief correctly.

The prosecutor delivers a speech that is a masterpiece of social prosecution:

“I accuse this man of burying his mother with a criminal heart.”

A criminal heart. Not a violent act, not a provable intention, but the wrong emotional presentation at a moment when emotional presentation is socially mandatory.

Meursault is convicted not for what he did but for what he failed to perform.

Camus is making a point about social conformity as moral demand: the way societies require not just behavioral compliance but emotional compliance, the performance of appropriate feeling at appropriate moments, under penalty of being classified as inhuman, as dangerous, as other.

The man who weeps at his mother’s funeral, then kills, might be acquitted. The man who does not weep, then kills, must be executed, because his non-weeping has revealed him to be outside the social contract, outside the community of feeling, and therefore not protected by its norms.

V. Meursault and the Absurd

Camus published The Myth of Sisyphus in the same year as The Stranger, 1942.

They are companion texts. The Myth is the philosophy; The Stranger is the philosophy embodied.

The Absurd, for Camus, is not a property of the world. It is not a property of human beings. It is the confrontation between the two, between the human need for meaning, clarity, unity and the world’s complete, indifferent silence in response.

We demand that the world make sense. The world does not answer. The gap between the demand and the silence, this is the Absurd.

Meursault, in the first part of the novel, is not yet an absurd hero in Camus’s full sense. He is pre-philosophical, living without reflection, inhabiting sensation without analyzing it, neither demanding meaning nor noticing its absence.

It is the trial, the death sentence, the chaplain, that transforms him.

In the final pages, the prison chaplain visits Meursault and insists that he must turn to God, that he cannot face death without faith, that his indifference is a kind of fear he will not admit.

Meursault’s response is the most important passage in the novel:

“I had been right, I was still right, I was always right. I had lived my life one way and I could just as well have lived it another. I had done this and I hadn’t done that. I hadn’t done this thing but I had done another. And so? As if all that waiting had been waiting for this moment and this dawn and this release.”

He grabs the chaplain by the collar. He screams at him.

And in the screaming, something is released. Not faith, not conversion, not regret, but a kind of fierce, implacable acceptance.

He is going to die. The universe does not care.

This is true for everyone: the chaplain, the prosecutor, the people who wept at his trial, all of them are going to die, all of them live under a death sentence, all of them inhabit a universe that will not answer their demand for meaning.

The difference is that Meursault knows it and will not pretend otherwise.

“As if that blind rage had washed me clean, rid me of hope; and, gazing up at the dark sky spangled with its signs and stars, for the first time, the first, I laid my heart open to the gentle indifference of the world.”

The gentle indifference of the world.

La tendre indifférence du monde.

This is the novel’s emotional and philosophical climax. Not despair. Not nihilism. A kind of peace, hard-won, unsentimental, clear-eyed, that comes from finally stopping the demand, finally accepting that the world will not answer, finally opening to the silence not as a wound but as a condition.

And finding, in that acceptance, something that feels like freedom.

VI. The Postcolonial Problem

Any honest reading of The Stranger must confront what the novel does not do.

The Arab Meursault kills has no name. In 123 pages, he has no name. He has a sister, briefly mentioned. He has a body, on a beach, under the sun. He is killed. He does not speak. He does not exist as a subject in the novel’s moral universe.

This is not an accident. It is the structural condition of the novel, and it is the novel’s most serious moral failure.

Kamel Daoud’s The Meursault Investigation (2013) gives the Arab a name: Musa. Gives him a mother who grieves. Gives him a brother who narrates his absence.

It is a remarkable act of literary justice, taking the shadow at the center of Camus’s novel and making it a person.

The question the postcolonial reading poses: can the novel’s philosophical achievement be separated from its colonial blindness?

Can we read Meursault’s absurd heroism, his refusal to lie, his acceptance of the indifferent universe, while holding at the same time the fact that the indifference extends to the Arab’s life, which the novel treats as philosophically weightless?

I do not think this question has a clean answer.

Camus was not a racist in any simple sense. His journalism on the treatment of Algerians was among the most courageous in French Algeria. He opposed the death penalty. He opposed torture.

But he was a product of his moment and his place, a pied-noir, a French Algerian, writing within a literary tradition that did not require him to see the Arab as a subject.

The novel’s philosophical power and its moral blindness are not separable. They are the same structure, the same capacity to focus on the individual consciousness while rendering invisible the structural conditions that make that consciousness possible.

This does not make the novel less great. It makes it more complicated.

Great art is often like this: the flaw is not separable from the achievement. The thing that makes it powerful is related to the thing that makes it troubling.

Read it knowing this. Read Daoud alongside it.

VII. What Meursault Is Not

He is not a role model.

Camus was explicit about this, and was frustrated by readers who took Meursault’s radical present-tense honesty as an ethical ideal.

The absurd hero, for Camus, does not kill Arabs on beaches.

The absurd hero maintains the tension: knows that life is without ultimate meaning, and chooses to live fully anyway, in solidarity with other human beings, with rebellion, with passion, with justice.

Meursault has the first part, the acceptance of the indifferent universe, but not the second. He is not a model of engagement. He is a model of a certain kind of honesty that is necessary but not sufficient.

The Stranger is the diagnosis. The Myth of Sisyphus is the prescription. The Plague (1947) is the application, the absurd hero who knows the world is indifferent and chooses, in full knowledge of that indifference, to fight the plague.

VIII. The Sentence

Before I finish, the prose.

The Stranger in French is one of the most precisely calibrated prose styles in the literature.

Stuart Gilbert’s English translation (1946) softened it. Matthew Ward’s translation (1988) restored its austerity.

The difference between them is the difference between a photograph slightly out of focus and the same photograph in perfect clarity. The content is the same. The experience is not.

Ward preserves the flatness, the parataxis, the emotional neutrality of Camus’s French. The style is the philosophy. A more lyrical translation would be a more beautiful novel and a less truthful one.

“Mother died today.”

Not: “Maman died today.”

One word. The translator’s choice to use Mother rather than the French Maman, the more intimate, childlike word, changes the emotional register entirely.

Ward keeps Maman. Because Camus wrote Maman. Because the word matters.

IX. Why It Stays

I have returned to The Stranger many times.

Each time, I read it differently, because I am different, because what I bring to Meursault changes what I find in him.

At twenty, I read it as liberation. The permission to not perform, to live in the body and the present, to refuse the social demand for appropriate feeling.

Later, I read it as warning. The cost of a life without connection, without the willingness to build the bridges that feeling, expressed, makes possible.

Later still, I read it as the novel about honesty. The most radical kind of honesty, the honesty that is not tactical or selective but constitutional, the honesty that cannot be turned off even when turning it off would save your life.

None of these readings is wrong. All of them are incomplete.

The novel holds them all at once, which is what great novels do. They do not deliver a message. They sustain a tension.

The tension in The Stranger:

between the freedom of not pretending and the cost of being incapable of pretending.

Between the peace of accepting the indifferent universe and the violence it takes to arrive at that peace.

Between the man who will not lie and the Arab whose death that honesty cannot account for.

Between the novel’s philosophical achievement and its moral blind spot.

Camus knew all of this. He was twenty-eight when he wrote it.

“In the midst of winter, I found there was, within me, an invincible summer.”

He wrote that too. Later. After everything.

Read The Stranger first. Then The Myth of Sisyphus. Then The Plague. Then Kamel Daoud’s The Meursault Investigation. Then go back to The Stranger.

It will be a different book. You will be a different reader. This is the point.

item.title: The Philosopher's Nephew: On Nepotism, Merit, and the Betrayal of Ideas
item.description:
In 347 BCE, Plato died.

He was eighty years old. He had founded the Academy (the first institution of higher learning in the Western world) and run it for forty years.

He left it to his nephew.

Speusippus.

Not to Aristotle, who had studied at the Academy for twenty years, who was by universal agreement the most brilliant mind in Athens, who would go on to write the Organon, the Physics, the Metaphysics, the Nicomachean Ethics, the Poetics, the Politics.

The man who would, in short, produce more original philosophy than any human being before or since.

Not to Aristotle.

To the nephew.

Speusippus was Plato’s sister’s son. He was a competent philosopher. He wrote works that are now almost entirely lost, and their loss, frankly, has not been felt the way the loss of Aristotle’s early dialogues has been felt.

He led the Academy for eight years. It declined under his leadership.

Aristotle left Athens. He traveled, did biological research, tutored the young Alexander of Macedon, and eventually returned to Athens to found his own school: the Lykeion.

There, walking in the covered walkways (peripatos, hence the Peripatetics), he produced the body of work that shaped Western thought for two thousand years.

Plato’s nepotism gave us the Lyceum.

This is the most expensive act of favoritism in the history of ideas.

I. What Nepotism Is

Nepotism, from the Italian nipote (nephew), entered English in the 17th century to describe the practice of popes appointing their nephews to positions of power.

The etymology is precise. Nipote derives from Latin nepos, nephew, the same root as nephew in English.

The popes were systematic about it. Several Renaissance popes appointed multiple nephews as cardinals, creating dynasties of ecclesiastical power based on blood rather than virtue.

The practice was so common that it was considered a fact of life rather than a scandal.

But the word captures something older and more universal:

The preference for the familiar over the excellent. The replacement of merit by connection. The substitution of “who you are” for “what you can do.”

Plato did not call it nepotism. He did not need to. It was simply what he did.

II. Plato’s Contradiction

Here is the irony that history has not been kind enough to highlight:

Plato wrote, at length, about the philosopher-king, the ruler who governs by knowledge, not by birth or wealth or connection.

He wrote about the meritocratic selection of guardians in the Republic: the careful testing of candidates, the long education, the rigorous evaluation.

He wrote about the Form of the Good, the highest object of knowledge, accessible only to those who had done the work, followed the argument, earned the understanding.

He built an institution dedicated to this ideal.

And then he gave the institution to his nephew.

The gap between the philosophy and the practice is one of the most instructive moments in the history of ideas.

Not because Plato was a hypocrite, though he was, in this instance, but because it shows how deeply the instinct toward nepotism runs.

Even the philosopher who articulated the most rigorous theory of merit in the ancient world could not, when the moment came, override the pull of blood.

III. Aristotle’s Response

Aristotle did not write about this directly.

He was too careful, too formal, too committed to the appearance of impartiality in his philosophical writing.

But his response was unmistakable:

He left.

He did not protest, did not argue, did not try to reform the Academy from within.

He built something new.

The Lyceum was, in many ways, a deliberate contrast to the Academy.

The Academy focused on mathematics and Platonic forms; Aristotle focused on observation, classification, the study of living things.

The Academy was elite and restricted; Aristotle lectured publicly, in the morning to advanced students, in the evening to general audiences.

As the Academy became increasingly mystical under Speusippus, Aristotle became increasingly empirical.

The Lyceum had a library, the first research library in history. A collection of biological specimens. Students doing fieldwork: collecting data on constitutions of city-states, dissecting animals, observing tidal patterns.

Aristotle created the model of the research university two thousand years before the research university existed.

And he did it because he was excluded from the institution he should have led.

IV. The Taxonomy of Nepotism

Plato’s case is ancient and obvious. The modern versions are more subtle.

Academic nepotism.

The advisor who steers the best postdoc positions to their own students, regardless of quality.

The hiring committee that advances the candidate who went to the right school, who knows the right people, who shares the committee’s research agenda, rather than the candidate who would most advance the field.

The journal editor who fast-tracks papers from colleagues and collaborators, who sends difficult papers to hostile reviewers and friendly papers to sympathetic ones.

The grant committee that funds established names (safe, credentialed, well-connected) rather than risky, unconventional, potentially revolutionary work.

None of these is called nepotism. They are called “quality assessment,” “cultural fit,” “network effects,” “track record evaluation.”

The outcome is the same: merit is subordinated to connection.

Institutional nepotism.

The department that has not hired outside its own PhD graduates in thirty years.

The research group that has become an intellectual dynasty, where the founder’s ideas are reproduced but never challenged, where the students who stay are the ones who agree, where the students who leave are the ones who think differently.

The conference circuit where the same names appear on the same panels year after year, not because no one else has anything to say but because the network is closed.

Intellectual nepotism.

Perhaps the most insidious form.

The preference for ideas from familiar sources. The tendency to cite the same authorities. The dismissal of work from outside the network as “not rigorous,” “not relevant,” “not serious,” when what is really meant is “not from us.”

The peer review system, intended to be meritocratic, is undermined by the fact that the community of peers is itself structured by network effects.

We review, hire, cite, and fund each other.

The system is not corrupt in the simple sense. No money changes hands, no laws are broken. It is corrupt in the structural sense: the outputs reflect the network as much as they reflect the merit.

V. Why It Happens: The Psychology

Nepotism is not primarily a moral failure. It is a cognitive one.

The first cause is familiarity bias. We trust what we know, are more comfortable with the familiar. The candidate who went to our institution, knows our colleagues, uses our vocabulary feels more legible, more trustworthy, more likely to succeed. This feeling is often wrong. But it is reliable.

Then risk aversion. Choosing the unknown is risky. If the unconventional hire fails, you are blamed; if the conventional hire fails, you shrug. You made the reasonable choice. Nepotism is risk management; it distributes blame safely.

Confirmation bias compounds the rest. We evaluate candidates through the lens of what we already believe success looks like, so the brilliant outsider (who approaches the problem differently, who has read different books, who comes from a different tradition) looks wrong. Not because they are wrong. Because they don’t fit the template.

And reciprocity holds it all together. Academic networks run on exchange. I support your student, you support mine. I review your paper, you review mine. The conference invitations are traded back and forth. This is not corruption. It is social fabric. But it has the same effect as corruption: resources flow along network lines rather than merit lines.

VI. The Cost

What does nepotism cost?

The obvious cost: the brilliant outsider who does not get the position, the funding, the platform.

The Aristotle who must leave and build something new, if they are lucky enough, talented enough, resilient enough to do so.

Many are not.

The cost that is harder to measure: what is not done.

The research that is not funded because it challenges established paradigms. The ideas that are not developed because the people who had them were excluded from the institutions where development happens. The revolutions that do not occur, or occur decades late, because the revolutionary could not get a position.

We cannot measure this cost. We do not know what we have lost.

We only know, in retrospect, when someone escaped the system, when an Einstein worked in a patent office, when an Aristotle founded his own school, and produced work that the establishment missed.

We do not know how many could not escape, how many gave up, how many adjusted their thinking to fit what was fundable, publishable, acceptable, and lost whatever was original in them.

This is the true cost of nepotism: not the individual injustice, but the aggregate loss, the intellectual universe that did not happen.

VII. The Meritocracy Illusion

Here I need to complicate the argument.

Pure meritocracy does not exist. It has never existed. It cannot exist, for reasons that are structural, not merely practical.

Merit is not objective. What counts as merit depends on what you are measuring, who is doing the measuring, and what framework they use.

In a field dominated by one paradigm, “merit” means “excellence within that paradigm.” Work that challenges the paradigm does not look meritorious; it looks confused, underdeveloped, irrelevant.

Kuhn’s Structure of Scientific Revolutions describes this: normal science evaluates by the standards of the paradigm, while revolutionary science is, by definition, incommensurable with those standards.

The revolutionary looks like a bad scientist to those who measure by the existing paradigm.

Social capital is also part of merit. A researcher who communicates well, who presents compellingly, who networks effectively is, in practical terms, more productive than an equally brilliant researcher who cannot communicate.

Is this merit or connection? Both. The line is blurry.

And early advantage compounds. The student who goes to the best undergraduate institution gets access to the best graduate programs. The graduate student who gets the best advisor gets access to the best positions. The early career researcher who gets the first grant gets the data for the next grant.

Inequality of opportunity becomes, over time, the appearance of inequality of merit.

I am not arguing against merit. I am arguing that “we hired on merit” is often self-deception, the comfortable belief that our preferences are objective evaluations, that our networks are just the natural result of quality seeking quality.

They are not. They are networks. Networks have structure. Structure produces path-dependence. Path-dependence produces oligarchy.

VIII. What Can Be Done

I want to be honest here. I do not have clean solutions.

But I have observations.

Blind review works.

When orchestras began conducting blind auditions (candidates behind a screen), the proportion of women hired increased dramatically.

The reviewers were not sexist in their intentions; they were biased in their evaluations. Removing the identity removed the bias.

Blind peer review, blind grant review, blind hiring where feasible: these are imperfect (in small fields, people recognize work by style), but they are better than the alternative.

Diversity of network is a quality signal, not a compromise.

A department that has hired only from three institutions for thirty years has a problem, not a diversity problem in the political sense but an intellectual one.

Intellectual monocultures are fragile. They produce sophisticated elaboration of a small set of ideas.

The most productive intellectual environments in history (Bell Labs, the Cavendish Laboratory, the Vienna Circle, the Manhattan Project) were characterized by radical intellectual diversity: people from different traditions, different countries, different disciplines, arguing fiercely with each other.

Diversity is not charity. It is quality insurance.

Transparency about process matters.

The most powerful antidote to nepotism is accountability, the requirement that decisions be explained, that criteria be stated, that evaluations be documented.

Nepotism thrives in opacity. “We just felt they were the right fit” is the language of networks doing what networks do, disguised as judgment.

Force the judgment into language. Language has to be defensible. Defensibility constrains bias.

And cultivate epistemic humility.

The deepest cause of nepotism is the conviction that we know what excellence looks like, that our template for quality is the template for quality.

This conviction is almost always wrong.

The history of science and philosophy is the history of excellence looking nothing like what was expected.

Darwin was a failed medical student. Einstein failed to get an academic position. Ramanujan had no formal training. Barbara McClintock was ignored for thirty years.

Excellence is not well-behaved. It does not arrive credentialed. It does not respect your network.

The institutions that found it were the ones willing to be surprised, willing to look at something unfamiliar and ask is this good? rather than is this like us?

IX. Back to Plato

I want to return to Plato, because his case is not simply a failure. It is a paradox.

Plato was, in many respects, one of the most radical meritocrats in history.

His vision of the ideal state (the philosopher-king selected by merit, the guardians chosen through rigorous testing, the gold and silver and bronze souls sorted by their nature) is one of the most thoroughgoing anti-aristocratic visions in ancient thought.

He rejected hereditary rule. He rejected wealth as a qualification. He proposed, in an Athens that confined women to the household, that women could be guardians and philosophers.

And then he gave the Academy to his nephew.

What do we do with this?

Not: Plato was a hypocrite, therefore ignore him.

But: Plato was human, which means his ideals and his instincts were in tension, and his instincts won at the crucial moment.

This is not Plato’s failure alone. It is the human condition.

We all believe in merit (in the abstract, in principle, when it is not our nephew, our student, our colleague, our tradition on the line).

When it is: the instinct toward the familiar, the trusted, the connected is very strong.

Stronger, often, than principle.

The question is not: are you capable of nepotism?

You are. We all are.

The question is: have you built systems that constrain your instincts when they conflict with your values?

Plato had not.

We should.

X. The Aristotle Lesson

Aristotle’s response to being passed over is the most important part of this story.

He did not become bitter, or if he did, did not stay bitter. He refused to compromise his intellectual standards to make himself acceptable to Speusippus. He did not spend his energy trying to correct the injustice, trying to get what he deserved.

He built.

He took what he knew, what he had learned in twenty years at the Academy, and he built something new, something that reflected his own vision rather than Plato’s.

The Lyceum was not a better Academy. It was a different thing entirely.

And it produced work that the Academy, under any leadership, could not have produced, because Aristotle’s empirical, systematic, encyclopedic approach to knowledge was fundamentally different from Plato’s mathematical, formal, idealist approach.

The nepotism that excluded Aristotle gave us both the Academy and the Lyceum, the Platonic and the Aristotelian traditions, the mathematical and the empirical approaches to knowledge.

History is strange.

The injustice produced richness.

I am not recommending injustice.

I am noting that the person who responds to exclusion by building, rather than by seeking revenge, or adjusting to fit, or abandoning the work,

is the person who matters.

Aristotle mattered.

Speusippus is a footnote.

Coda

Every institution has its Speusippus.

The nephew who got the position. The connected candidate who got the grant. The well-networked mediocrity who got the platform.

Every field has its Aristotle, or had one, once.

The brilliant outsider who was passed over. Who left, or was forced out, or simply was never let in.

Some of them built their own Lyceum. Many did not.

We do not know what we lost when they did not.

We know what we gained when they did.

The lesson is simple. The practice is hard.

Judge by ideas rather than networks, by work rather than credentials, by what is in front of you rather than by familiarity.

And when you cannot, when the instinct toward the familiar wins, at least be honest about what you are doing.

Don’t call it quality assessment. Call it what it is.

Plato didn’t call it anything. He just did it.

Two and a half thousand years later, we still remember.

Not him for doing it, but Aristotle, for what he built despite it.

Further reading:

Plato. Republic (trans. Grube/Reeve). The foundational text on meritocracy, guardians, and philosopher-kings.

Diogenes Laërtius. Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The ancient biographical sources on Speusippus, Aristotle, and the Academy.

Jonathan Barnes. Aristotle: A Very Short Introduction. The best brief account of Aristotle’s achievement.

Pierre Bourdieu. Homo Academicus (1984). The foundational sociological study of academic nepotism; brutal and accurate.

Robert Merton. “The Matthew Effect in Science” (1968). Science 159, 56. The foundational paper on cumulative advantage.

Sheila Slaughter & Larry Leslie. Academic Capitalism (1997). How market pressures distort academic merit.

item.title: Sartre: Existence Precedes Essence, and That Is Terrifying
item.description:
Jean-Paul Sartre walked into a café in Paris and watched the waiter.

The waiter’s movements were too precise, too perfectly waiter-like. He carried his tray with a rigidity that was almost theatrical. His walk, his tone, his attentiveness, all of it performed with a slightly excessive care, as if he were playing the role of waiter rather than being a waiter.

Sartre watched him and thought: this man is in bad faith.

Not because he is lying, and not because he is a bad person. Because he is pretending, to himself and to the world, that he is a waiter in the same way a rock is a rock.

As if his identity were fixed, as if he had no choice, as if the role explained the man rather than the man choosing the role.

This moment, in a Paris café, watching an ordinary man do his job, became one of the most famous examples in the history of philosophy.

Because it points to something Sartre believed with absolute conviction:

You are never just what you are.

You are always also the one who chose it, and who could choose otherwise.

I. The Man

Jean-Paul Sartre was born in Paris in 1905.

His father died when he was fifteen months old. His mother returned to her parents’ house. He grew up in the library of his grandfather, Charles Schweitzer (uncle of Albert Schweitzer), surrounded by books, convinced from childhood that literature was the highest calling.

He was, by most accounts, not physically attractive: short, wall-eyed, increasingly blind. He compensated with a ferocious intelligence and an extraordinary capacity for work.

He studied philosophy at the École Normale Supérieure, where he met Simone de Beauvoir, his partner, intellectual companion, and the most important relationship of his life.

They never married. They maintained a relationship of radical honesty, transparent about their other relationships, committed to each other without possession. Whether this worked, for de Beauvoir, is a question the letters complicate.

He was drafted in World War II, captured by the Germans in 1940, held in a prisoner of war camp for nine months. He was released, apparently on medical grounds, and returned to Paris, where he wrote philosophy and plays while the city was occupied.

After the war, he became the most famous intellectual in France, perhaps in the world.

He refused the Nobel Prize in 1964. He said that accepting it would compromise the independence of the writer.

He died in 1980, nearly blind, exhausted, still writing, still engaged, refusing to be reduced to what he had been.

II. Existence Precedes Essence

The central claim of Sartrean existentialism is condensed in a single phrase:

Existence precedes essence.

To understand what this means, consider a paper knife.

A paper knife is made by an artisan who has a concept of the knife before making it: a purpose, a design, an essence. The essence precedes the existence. The knife exists in order to cut paper. Its being is determined by its function.

For centuries, theistic philosophy applied this logic to human beings: God created humans with a purpose, a nature, an essence. Human beings exist in order to fulfill this divine design. The essence precedes the existence.

Sartre removes God.

Without God, there is no prior conception of the human. There is no factory blueprint, no divine intention, no human nature in the traditional sense.

Human beings simply appear, thrown into existence, without prior purpose or predetermined nature, and then must decide what they are.

“Man first of all exists, encounters himself, surges up in the world, and defines himself afterwards.”

You are not a human being with a fixed nature who then makes choices within that nature. You are the choices you make: the sum of your acts, your commitments, your projects.

“Man is nothing else but what he makes of himself.”

This is the most liberating and the most terrifying sentence in existentialist philosophy.

Liberating: you are not fixed. Your past does not determine you. Your family, your culture, your psychology, none of these are your destiny. You can always choose otherwise.

Terrifying: there is no excuse. There is no nature to blame, no God, no circumstances sufficient to explain why you are what you are.

You have chosen, you are choosing, you will choose.

III. Radical Freedom and Its Weight

Sartre’s freedom is not the freedom of pleasant choices.

It is radical freedom: freedom that cannot be escaped, freedom that is itself a burden.

“We are condemned to be free.”

The word condemned is precise. Not gifted with freedom, not blessed by it. Condemned to it.

The condemnation: you cannot not choose. Refusing to choose, following orders, acting out of habit: each of these is a choice in disguise.

There is no alibi.

This is what makes existence anguish, Sartre’s term for the fundamental anxiety of recognizing your own freedom.

When you stand at the edge of a cliff, there is a specific anxiety: not just the fear of falling, but the recognition that you could jump. Nothing prevents you but yourself. The abyss opens not below you but within you.

Anguish, in Sartre, is the recognition that nothing compels me to be what I am.

You might not jump. You almost certainly won’t. But the recognition that you could is the existential structure of freedom: the choice is always there, and you are always the one holding yourself back.

IV. Bad Faith

If radical freedom is the truth of human existence, if you are always choosing and responsible and the author of what you are, why do so many people act as if they are not?

Because freedom is unbearable.

Bad faith (mauvaise foi) is Sartre’s name for the various strategies by which human beings flee from their freedom, by which they convince themselves that they are not really choosing, but determined, with no option.

The waiter who is too perfectly a waiter, he is in bad faith. He is pretending that his role defines him completely, that the waiter is what he is, rather than what he does.

The woman on a date who ignores the unambiguous romantic intentions of her companion, she is in bad faith. She does not want to acknowledge the situation because acknowledging it would require a choice. So she pretends not to see it.

The person who says “I had no choice,” who uses their psychology, their upbringing, their past as a complete explanation for their present, is in bad faith.

These are not moral failures exactly. They are failures of honesty: the refusal to acknowledge what one actually is, a being who is always choosing, with full freedom and full responsibility.

Bad faith is the attempt to flee what cannot be fled.

V. The Look

One of Sartre’s most striking contributions to philosophy is his analysis of the Look (le regard).

Imagine you are alone. You are doing something you would not do if anyone were watching, looking through a keyhole, perhaps.

Then you hear footsteps. You sense someone behind you.

In that moment, something happens.

You are suddenly seen. And being seen transforms you, from the free subject experiencing the world to an object in someone else’s world.

The Look of the Other fixes you, temporarily and uncomfortably, as a thing. It assigns you an identity, a nature, a description.

“Hell is other people.”

This is the most misquoted line in Sartre, usually taken to mean that other people are unpleasant, which is not what he meant.

It means: other people’s gaze is a kind of hell because it threatens to fix you as an object, to reduce your radical freedom to a thing with properties.

The waiter, the coward, the saint: these are descriptions others use to reduce you. You are always more than any description. But the Look presses you toward the description, and the constant negotiation between what you are for yourself and what you are for others is one of the fundamental tensions of human existence.

VI. Authenticity

If bad faith is the flight from freedom, authenticity is its opposite: the honest acknowledgment of your freedom, your responsibility, your situation.

Authenticity is not a moral code. Sartre is explicit: there are no objective values, no given moral rules, no external standard by which to judge choices.

Authenticity is a formal value. It describes the quality of the relation between the agent and their choices, not the content of the choices themselves.

The authentic person chooses, knowing they are choosing, knowing the choice is theirs and cannot be blamed on God or nature or psychology or culture.

They choose and they own the choice.

This does not mean anything goes.

In his lecture “Existentialism is a Humanism” (1945), Sartre argued that in choosing for oneself, one implicitly chooses for all humanity, because to choose is to assert that the chosen value is worthy of choice, and therefore worthy for anyone in a similar situation.

“When we choose, we choose for all humanity.”

This is existentialism’s attempt to generate moral seriousness without moral realism, to preserve responsibility and obligation in a world without God, without fixed human nature, without objective values.

Whether it succeeds is debated. That it takes the problem seriously is not.

VII. Sartre and History

Sartre’s later work moved increasingly toward Marxism, an attempt to synthesize existentialism with a structural account of history and class.

The Critique of Dialectical Reason (1960) is his most ambitious and most difficult work, an attempt to ground Marxist historical analysis in the existentialist account of human freedom.

The basic problem he was trying to solve: existentialism emphasizes individual freedom and responsibility. Marxism emphasizes structural determination: class, history, material conditions.

How do you hold both?

Sartre’s answer, echoing Marx: human beings make history, but not in conditions of their own choosing. Freedom is always situated, always operating within structures that it did not create and cannot simply transcend.

The poor person is free, but their freedom is exercised in conditions of scarcity and oppression that constrain what their freedom can mean.

This is a genuine advance on pure existentialism. Freedom is not abstract. It has different weights in different conditions. The philosophical task is not just to describe freedom but to fight for the conditions in which freedom becomes real.

VIII. Being and Nothingness

Sartre’s major philosophical work, Being and Nothingness (1943), written and published while Paris was under German occupation, is one of the most difficult books in the philosophical canon.

Seven hundred pages of dense phenomenology, written in a style that is at once rigorous and literary, systematic and full of brilliant examples.

Its central distinction:

Being-in-itself (en-soi): The being of things, rocks, tables, paper knives. Dense, self-identical, complete. A rock is what it is. Fully. Without remainder. No gap between what it is and what it is.

Being-for-itself (pour-soi): The being of consciousness, human being. Always ahead of itself, projecting, negating what it is.

Consciousness is defined by nothingness, the gap, the lack, the not-yet, the always-exceeding of any fixed identity.

“Consciousness is a being such that in its being, its being is in question.”

You are not what you are. You are what you are not yet. The project of becoming is always you, the movement toward a future that, when reached, will already be past.

This is the formal structure of freedom: not the absence of determination, but the presence of nothingness, the gap between what you are and what you will be that is the space of choice.

IX. What Sartre Gets Right

The deepest contribution of Sartrean existentialism is the absolute refusal of the alibi.

We live in a culture of explanation. Every behavior has its cause, every failure its context. This is valuable: understanding causation matters. But Sartre preserves something that pure determinism loses, which is the reality of responsibility.

You are, within limits, the author of what you are. The limits are real and they matter. But within them, you choose. And the choosing is yours.

He also insists that identity is a project, not a possession. You are not your past, your type, your sign, your diagnosis. You are not your nationality, your class, your family. These are things you have been. What you will be is not yet determined. This is either terrifying or liberating, depending on what you were hoping your past would excuse you from.

And he insists on the seriousness of freedom. In a world where algorithms predict your choices, neuroscience explains your decisions, and your behavior seems the inevitable product of genes and environment, Sartre says: you are choosing. You are responsible. The universe does not excuse you.

This is uncomfortable. It is also the most serious respect one human being can pay to another.

X. The Café, Again

The waiter in the café, he goes home at night. He takes off the waiter’s jacket. He is no longer performing the role.

What is he then?

Sartre’s answer: exactly what he chooses to be. A husband, perhaps. A father. A reader. A man who worries about his mother. A man who sometimes laughs at things no one else finds funny.

He is none of these fully. He is always exceeding each of them.

He is the nothingness at the heart of being, the gap, the freedom, the not-yet.

“Man is not what he is, and he is what he is not.”

This sentence is not a paradox to be dissolved. It is a description of what it is to be human:

To be the being who is never simply what it is, who is always more than any description, who is always choosing, responsible, free,

even when freedom is the last thing it wants to be.

Further reading:

Sartre’s lecture Existentialism is a Humanism (1945) is the shortest entry point, readable in one evening.

The full philosophical work Being and Nothingness (1943) is the one to take next, when ready.

The novel Nausea (1938) contains the same ideas in narrative form.

Simone de Beauvoir’s The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947) is the strongest development of existentialist ethics.

Sarah Bakewell’s At the Existentialist Café (2016) is the most readable introduction to the whole movement.

item.title: Nietzsche: God Is Dead, and We Have Killed Him
item.description:
In 1882, a madman ran into a marketplace.

It was broad daylight. He was carrying a lantern.

He cried: “I seek God! I seek God!”

The people around him laughed. Has God got lost? Did he go on a voyage?

The madman turned on them:

“Where is God? I will tell you. We have killed him — you and I. All of us are his murderers. But how did we do this? How could we drink up the sea? Who gave us the sponge to wipe away the entire horizon? What were we doing when we unchained this earth from its sun? Whither is it moving now? Whither are we moving? Away from all suns? Are we not plunging continually? Backward, sideward, forward, in all directions? Is there still any up or down? Are we not straying as through an infinite nothing? Do we not feel the breath of empty space? Has it not become colder? Is not night continually closing in on us?”

He paused.

“I have come too early. This tremendous event is still on its way. It has not yet reached the ears of men.”

Friedrich Nietzsche wrote this in 1882. We are still catching up.

I. The Most Misread Philosopher

Nietzsche is the most misread philosopher in the Western tradition.

He has been claimed by Nazis, by self-help culture, by nihilists. All wrongly.

His sister Elisabeth, an antisemite who married into the German nationalist movement, falsified his letters and sold his name to the Third Reich. The self-help industry strips his aphorisms of context and pastes them onto motivational posters. The nihilists stop at the death of God without reading what came after.

He has been used to justify domination, cruelty, nationalism, and the worship of strength.

He would have been contemptuous of all of it.

He wrote: “I am not a man, I am dynamite.”

He meant: his philosophy, properly understood, would explode every comfortable assumption, including the comfortable assumptions of those who thought they were his followers.

To read Nietzsche is to be made uncomfortable. If you are not uncomfortable, you are not reading him.

II. The Man

Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was born in 1844 in Röcken, Prussia, the son of a Lutheran pastor who died of brain disease when Nietzsche was four years old.

He was a prodigy: appointed professor of classical philology at the University of Basel at twenty-four, before he had even completed his doctorate.

He was a close friend of Richard Wagner, a friendship that shaped his early work and whose disintegration shaped his mature work. When Wagner descended into German nationalism and Christian sentiment, Nietzsche broke with him completely and wrote some of the most savage criticism of Wagner’s later work ever composed.

He suffered from chronic, debilitating illness throughout his adult life: migraines, vision problems, digestive disorders. He wrote despite constant pain, often unable to read for more than an hour a day, dictating to assistants or writing in large script to spare his eyes.

In 1889, in Turin, he saw a horse being beaten. He threw his arms around the horse’s neck, collapsed, and never recovered his sanity.

He spent the last eleven years of his life in a state of mental collapse, first in an asylum, then in the care of his mother and sister.

He died in 1900, aged fifty-five.

The works that changed philosophy (Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil, The Genealogy of Morals, Twilight of the Idols, The Antichrist, Ecce Homo) were all written between 1883 and 1888.

Five years. In chronic pain. Nearly blind.

“What does not kill me makes me stronger.”

He meant it literally.

III. God Is Dead

“God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him.”

This is the most misunderstood statement in modern philosophy.

Nietzsche was not making an atheist argument. He was not saying: there is no God, therefore God is dead. He was saying something far more radical and far more frightening.

What has become unbelievable is the belief in God: the Christian God in particular, with the moral framework that depended on it, and the entire structure of values that had organized Western civilization for two thousand years.

It had not been refuted or disproven. It had become unbelievable.

The scientific revolution, the Enlightenment, the historical criticism of the Bible: these had not exactly proved God false. They had made it impossible to believe in God in the way people had believed for centuries, with the naive, unreflective certainty that the cosmos had a moral structure and human life a divinely guaranteed purpose, that suffering had meaning and death was not the end.

This is what Nietzsche means by the death of God.

And the consequences, which he saw with terrifying clarity, were not liberation. Not immediately.

The consequences were nihilism.

If God is dead, if the moral order that depended on God has collapsed, on what foundation do we build values? What stops the conclusion that nothing matters?

The madman’s terror is real. He is not celebrating. He is mourning, and warning.

“The greatest recent event — that God is dead, that the belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable — is already beginning to cast its first shadows over Europe.”

The shadows are nihilism: the recognition that the old values have collapsed before new values have been found.

IV. The Will to Power

Nietzsche’s concept of the will to power (Wille zur Macht) is the most misunderstood concept in his philosophy.

It does not mean the desire to dominate others, political power, violence, or conquest.

The will to power is Nietzsche’s account of the fundamental drive of all life: the drive toward self-overcoming, toward growth, toward the expansion of one’s capacities.

“What is good? — All that heightens the feeling of power, the will to power, power itself in man. What is bad? — All that proceeds from weakness.”

But power here means the power to create, overcome, grow, not the power to destroy or dominate.

The highest expression of the will to power is the artist, the creator, who does not dominate others but overcomes themselves, who takes the raw material of experience and shapes it into something new.

The Übermensch (the Overman, the Superman) is not a master race. It is the human being who has overcome herd morality, resentment, pettiness: someone who creates new values rather than inheriting old ones, and who affirms life fully and without reservation.

Nietzsche’s examples of people approaching the Übermensch: Goethe. Napoleon. Caesar. Not because of their power over others, but because of their power over themselves, their ability to contain and transform suffering and contradiction into creative force.

V. Master and Slave Morality

In The Genealogy of Morals (1887), Nietzsche proposed one of the most provocative accounts of the origins of morality ever written.

He distinguished between two fundamentally different types of moral evaluation:

Master morality. The strong, the noble, the powerful define good as what they are: vital, active, creative, proud. They define bad as what they are not: weak, passive, reactive, base. The evaluation starts with the self. “I am good. You are bad.”

Slave morality. The weak, the oppressed, the resentful cannot overcome the strong directly. So they revalue values. They define good as what they are: humble, meek, suffering, self-denying. They define evil as what the strong are: powerful, proud, vital. The evaluation starts with the other. “You are evil. Therefore I am good.”

Slave morality is born from resentment, ressentiment: the festering of impotent hatred into a moral system that makes a virtue of powerlessness.

Nietzsche’s claim, provocative and controversial, is that Christianity is the great vehicle of slave morality.

The beatitudes (blessed are the meek, the poor in spirit, the suffering) are, Nietzsche argues, the revenge of the weak on the strong, the transformation of powerlessness into a cosmic virtue.

“Christianity is Platonism for the people.”

This is not mere contempt. Nietzsche had enormous respect for the psychological sophistication of the Christian tradition: its mastery of the inner life, its understanding of suffering.

His argument is more precise: that the Christian moral framework, built on resentment and the denial of life, is incompatible with the full affirmation of existence that he believed was necessary.

VI. Eternal Recurrence

Nietzsche considered the thought of eternal recurrence his most important idea.

The thought experiment:

What if this life, this exact life, with all its suffering, joy, pettiness, and greatness, had to be lived again, infinitely?

Not a similar life. This life: pain, mistakes, losses, moments of grace, all of it repeated exactly, forever.

Could you affirm that?

Could you say yes, again, with joy rather than resignation, not because everything was perfect but because you loved it enough to want it eternally?

This is not a cosmological claim. Nietzsche is not saying the universe actually recurs.

It is a test: the most demanding possible test of one’s relationship to life.

If you live in a way that, faced with eternal recurrence, you would say yes, then you are living well.

If you would recoil, if the thought of reliving your life fills you with horror, then you are not living as you should.

“My formula for greatness in a human being is amor fati: that one wants nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity. Not merely bear what is necessary, still less conceal it, but love it.”

Amor fati: love of fate.

Stronger than acceptance, different from resignation.

The full, unconditional affirmation of everything that has happened and will happen, not because it is all good but because it is all yours, and you would not be without it.

VII. Apollonian and Dionysian

In his first book, The Birth of Tragedy (1872), written at twenty-seven, Nietzsche introduced a distinction that has shaped aesthetics ever since.

The Apollonian. Order, reason, form, clarity, individuation. The principle of the beautiful illusion: the dream, the image, the individual. Named for Apollo, god of light, reason, prophecy.

The Dionysian. Chaos, ecstasy, dissolution, the primal unity. The shattering of the individual into collective, ecstatic experience. Named for Dionysus, god of wine, frenzy, transformation.

Great tragedy (Greek tragedy) holds them both together. The Dionysian chaos is given Apollonian form. The Apollonian dream is penetrated by Dionysian truth.

Socrates, Nietzsche argued, killed tragedy by insisting that reason could explain everything, that the Dionysian darkness was merely ignorance to be dissolved by argument.

The Socratic optimism (the belief that knowledge leads to virtue, that reason leads to happiness) was, for Nietzsche, a symptom of cultural decline: the replacement of tragic wisdom (the full acknowledgment of suffering and darkness) with shallow rationalism (the belief that everything can be fixed by thinking harder).

He later revised this view, acknowledged that his own early Romanticism had distorted it. But the distinction between the Apollonian and Dionysian remains one of the most generative ideas in the philosophy of art.

VIII. Perspectivism

One of Nietzsche’s most important epistemological contributions is perspectivism.

There is no view from nowhere. There is no God’s-eye perspective, no neutral, objective standpoint from which reality can be seen as it truly is.

Every claim to knowledge is made from a perspective, shaped by the knower’s drives, interests, history, embodiment, culture.

“There are no facts, only interpretations.”

This is not relativism in the simple sense. It is not the claim that all perspectives are equally valid. Nietzsche was fiercely evaluative: some perspectives are richer, more encompassing, more life-affirming than others.

But the claim to a perspective-independent truth, the claim that one’s own view is simply objective, is self-deception.

The honest thinker acknowledges their perspective, takes responsibility for it, and does not hide behind the fiction of objectivity.

This has been enormously influential across philosophy of science, literary theory, feminist epistemology, the sociology of knowledge.

The insight that knowledge is situated, that the knower is never absent from what is known: this is Nietzsche’s epistemological legacy.

IX. He Did Not Comfort Me

I read Nietzsche the way I read Dostoevsky. Not to be reassured. To be caught.

I first read him as a teenager. That was the problem. I have come to think Nietzsche is something like a third-year course in a major. Like quantum mechanics in physics, or data structures or algorithms in computer science. Without the scaffolding to prepare you, the reading effort comes to nothing. Mine did. I read him too early, and what I read stayed half-finished. I would have been ready, perhaps, as a third-year philosophy student at İstanbul University. Even then I think I would have struggled.

I read him from the Hasan Âli Yücel klasikleri series. The translations were beautiful, careful, alive in Turkish.

A few lines have stayed with me ever since.

“He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.” From Twilight of the Idols.

“Insanity in individuals is something rare. But in groups, parties, nations and epochs, it is the rule.” From Beyond Good and Evil, which is the book of his I love most.

And a line that travels under his name, whether or not it sits in any of his published books: “And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music.” I read this as a child and recognized myself. When my family went to weddings I used to watch the dancing adults and think, Filiz, if there were no music, how funny they would all look. I had no name for what I was noticing. Years later I had one.

He is not polite or safe or academic. He arrives to shatter the lies you tell yourself.

Three things drew me first.

First, he does not forgive false morality. What people present as goodness, humility, virtue, sacrifice: sometimes underneath these big words, what Nietzsche finds is envy, fear, resentment, the wish to look better than one is. I have always loved that question. What is really under the big words? Nietzsche strips people naked. He strips you naked too, if you read honestly.

Second, his idea of self-overcoming. Not the cheap “be yourself” of the self-help shelf. Something harder: to create yourself, educate yourself, produce your own values rather than inheriting them. This connects, for me, to Martin Eden. I have always lived close to the conviction that I will not settle for the life given to me. I will construct myself.

Third, the prose. Nietzsche does not write like a textbook. The sentences are knives. The aphorisms are sharp. Sometimes poetry, sometimes insult. I love thinkers who are intellectual, literary, and dangerous all at once.

But I would not fully surrender to him.

What I object to most is that he sometimes belittles compassion too much. I admire strong, self-creating people, people of great mental ambition. But I cannot give myself entirely to a purely ruthless idea of “power.” Because inside me there is also the side of my grandmother, my anane: protective, attentive, taking human fragility seriously, refusing to look away from what is broken. What Nietzsche calls “weakness” in some places, I would call simply being human.

The aristocratic tone bothers me too. “I am not for everyone.” “Übermensch.” “Herd morality.” Aesthetically these are seductive, intellectually they have purchase. But ethically they are dangerous, and Nietzsche himself did not control how dangerous they would become. I can grant that not everyone is deep or honest or thinking without using that observation to legitimize crushing anyone.

What I love in him is that he exposes the people who invent morality to avoid looking weak. What I refuse is the reading where fragility is always lower, always something to overcome rather than something to honor.

So let me say it as I would say it:

I loved Nietzsche because he did not comfort me. He caught me in the act. I would not surrender to him completely, though, because sometimes the greatest human nobility is not strength. It is staying breakable and refusing to become ugly.

X. What Remains

The world Nietzsche described is more ours than his.

The moral certainties he watched collapsing have not been rebuilt. The naive religious answer is unavailable to most intellectually serious people. The naive rationalist answer (reason will provide) has not delivered. The questions about value, meaning, and what we owe each other remain open in the way he said they would.

He did not solve this. He named it. That is not nothing.

The diagnosis of resentment also remains. The pattern Nietzsche identified is still recognizable everywhere: making weakness into virtue, envy into morality, inability into religion. He saw it clearly, before most people knew what they were looking at.

And the test of eternal recurrence still works. Not as a cosmological claim. As a test. Faced with reliving your life exactly, in all its suffering and joy, all its mistakes and graces, could you say yes? Not because everything was good. Because it was yours, and you would not be without it.

If you could say yes, you are living well.

If the thought makes you recoil, something is wrong, and it is worth knowing where.

This is the demand of amor fati.

Nietzsche made that demand of himself in his last clear years, in chronic pain, nearly blind, writing the books that would survive him. He answered yes by the act of writing them. The answer cost him everything, possibly even his sanity.

But he did answer.

That is what remains.

Coda

“I know my fate. One day my name will be associated with the memory of something tremendous — a crisis without equal on earth, the most profound collision of conscience, a decision that was conjured up against everything that had been believed, demanded, hallowed so far. I am no man. I am dynamite.”

He was right that his name would be associated with something tremendous.

He could not have predicted what.

The uses of Nietzsche (the misuses, the distortions, the appropriations) are themselves a kind of testament to what he identified: the desperate human need for new values after the death of the old ones, and the danger of filling that void with the first strong voice that comes along.

He was dynamite. He did not control the explosion.

None of us does.

Further reading: Walter Kaufmann’s translations of Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil, and The Genealogy of Morals are the standard English versions. Kaufmann’s own Nietzsche: Philosopher, Psychologist, Antichrist (1950) is the book that rescued Nietzsche from his Nazi appropriation. Julian Young’s Friedrich Nietzsche: A Philosophical Biography (2010) is the most thorough recent biography.
