item.title: Marcus Aurelius: The Emperor Who Wrote to Himself
item.description:
The most powerful man in the world sat down at night and wrote notes to himself.

Not to be published, not to be read, not to instruct anyone or build a reputation or leave a legacy.

Just notes. Reminders. Rebukes. The private record of a man trying, every single day, to be better than he was.

Marcus Aurelius was Emperor of Rome from 161 to 180 CE. He commanded the largest army in the world. He governed perhaps fifty million people. He fought wars on the Danube for most of his reign, standing in mud and snow at the edge of empire while plague devastated his troops and his adopted family betrayed him.

And at night, in the tent or the palace, he wrote things like this:

“If you are distressed by anything external, the pain is not due to the thing itself, but to your estimate of it. And this you have the power to revoke at any moment.”

“The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.”

“Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one.”

He was writing to himself. He was failing, often, to live what he wrote. He kept writing anyway.

I. The Accident of History

The Meditations should not exist.

Marcus never intended them for publication. They are written in the second person, you, as self-address, self-command, self-rebuke. “You have done this wrong. Do not do it again. This is what you must remember. Do not forget.”

They were probably written in the last decade of his life, during the Marcomannic Wars on the northern frontier, in moments between military command and administrative duty.

They survived by accident. A manuscript tradition that is poorly understood, copied by monks who perhaps did not fully grasp what they were preserving: a Roman emperor’s private notebook, not his public philosophy.

We do not know their original title. Meditations is a later editorial invention. The Greek manuscripts call them Ta eis heauton, Things to Oneself.

That is the right title. These are things written to oneself. The most intimate philosophical document from the ancient world.

II. The Man Behind the Emperor

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was born in 121 CE to a wealthy Spanish-Roman family.

He was adopted by the Emperor Antoninus Pius, himself adopted by Hadrian, as part of a carefully engineered succession. He did not want to be emperor. He wanted to be a philosopher.

At twelve, he encountered Stoicism and was, by his own account, transformed. He slept on the ground. He wore rough clothing. He studied with the Stoic teacher Epictetus, or rather with the writings of Epictetus, whom he never met. Epictetus had died around 135 CE, when Marcus was still a boy, and the Discourses reached him later through his teacher Junius Rusticus.

Epictetus had been a slave. Marcus would become an emperor. Both were, in their different ways, unfree: Epictetus in body, Marcus in obligation. Both found in Stoicism the same answer: freedom is not the absence of constraint. Freedom is the right relationship to constraint.

When Antoninus Pius died in 161 CE, Marcus became emperor.

He immediately appointed his adoptive brother Lucius Verus as co-emperor, an act of unusual generosity and political wisdom. He did not want sole power. He had never wanted power at all.

He spent most of his reign doing what he least wanted to do, commanding armies, administering justice, managing the endless machinery of empire, and writing at night about why this was necessary and how to bear it without becoming what it could make you.

III. The Stoic Framework, Lived

The Meditations are not a systematic philosophy. They are Stoic philosophy applied, imperfectly, repeatedly, urgently, to the specific pressures of Marcus’s life.

The central Stoic framework appears again and again, in slightly different formulations, as if Marcus needed to remind himself of the same truths over and over:

The dichotomy of control:

“Of things, some are in our power and some are not. In our power are opinion, motivation, desire, aversion, in a word, whatever is of our own doing. Not in our power are our body, our reputation, office, and in a word, whatever is not of our own doing.”

This is Epictetus. Marcus returns to it constantly, because he constantly forgets it, or fails to live it, or finds it insufficient under pressure.

The present moment:

“Confine yourself to the present.”

“Do not disturb yourself by thinking of the whole of your life. Let not your thoughts range over the many and varied troubles which have come to you in the past and will come again in the future, but ask yourself with regard to every present difficulty: ‘What is there in this that is intolerable and beyond endurance?’”

Marcus is not a natural present-moment person. He worries. He ruminates. He rehearses disasters. He writes instructions to himself to stop, which means he has not stopped.

This is what makes the Meditations human. He is not reporting his achievements. He is recording his aspirations and his failures to meet them.

The view from above:

One of Marcus’s recurring techniques, which he may have learned from Epictetus, is the view from above: the deliberate imaginative act of seeing your life from a great height, or across a long span of time.

“Look at the past, empire succeeding empire, and from that, extrapolate the future. Nothing but the same things. You can’t escape this rhythm of history.”

“Observe constantly that all things take place by change, and accustom yourself to consider that the nature of the Universe loves nothing so much as to change the things which are, and to make new things like them.”

Everything passes. Everything is temporary. The empire you govern will be ruins. Your name will be forgotten. Your decisions, agonized over, argued about, the ones that kept you awake, will be dust.

This is not nihilism. It is the therapeutic use of impermanence, the Stoic practice of holding the long view to dissolve the urgency of the immediate.

If it will not matter in a thousand years, why let it consume you now?

IV. What He Was Fighting

Marcus does not name his enemies in the Meditations. But they are visible between the lines.

Anger.

He returns to anger again and again, the anger of a powerful man who is constantly frustrated, constantly disappointed, constantly surrounded by people who are lesser than what the situation demands.

“When you wake up in the morning, tell yourself: the people I deal with today will be meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, jealous and surly.”

This is not misanthropy. It is preparation, the Stoic practice of premeditatio malorum, the premeditation of evils. Expect the worst. Be grateful when it doesn’t arrive. When it does arrive, you are ready.

“The best revenge is not to be like your enemy.”

He writes this because he is tempted to be like his enemies. He is emperor. He could simply destroy them. He writes this to himself because he knows that destroying them would destroy something in him.

Distraction.

“People look for retreats for themselves, in the country, at the sea, in the hills. But this is altogether a sign of the most common sort of man, for it is in your power whenever you choose to retire into yourself.”

He has no retreat. He is always watched, always needed, always on. The retreat must be internal, the philosophical practice of withdrawing into the self that is truly one’s own.

The corruption of power.

This is perhaps the most remarkable thing about the Meditations: the explicit, repeated anxiety about what power does to people.

“Take care that you are not made into a Caesar, that you are not dyed with this dye, for such things happen. Keep yourself then simple, good, pure, serious, free from affectation, a friend of justice, a worshipper of the gods, kind, affectionate, strenuous in all proper acts.”

“Take care that you are not made into a Caesar.”

He is Caesar. He is the emperor. And he is warning himself against becoming what he already is.

Not a warning against the title, but against the transformation of character that the title produces: the habit of being obeyed, the assumption of one’s own importance, the insulation from honest feedback, the slow corruption of judgment by the deference of everyone around you.

He saw this happening. He wrote against it, to himself, alone, at night.

Whether the writing helped, whether he succeeded in not becoming a Caesar, history does not give us a clear answer. By most accounts, he governed well. By some accounts, he failed his son Commodus, allowing him to succeed despite knowing his character, and the result was catastrophic.

He was not perfect. He was trying.

V. On Death

Death is everywhere in the Meditations.

Not because Marcus was morbid, but because the Stoics believed that the correct relationship to death was the foundation of everything else.

“Think of yourself as dead. You have lived your life. Now take what’s left and live it properly.”

“Not to live as if you had endless years ahead of you. Death overshadows you. While you’re alive and able, be good.”

He watched people die constantly. Plague swept through his armies, his children died young, colleagues and friends disappeared. Death was not an abstraction for him.

He used it as a clarifying lens:

“Ask yourself at every moment, ‘Is this necessary?’”

If you are going to die, if everyone you know is going to die, if the empire itself will eventually be ruins, then the question of what is necessary becomes sharp and urgent.

Most of what we do is not necessary. Most of what we worry about, and most of what we want, is not necessary either.

What remains, when the unnecessary is stripped away?

Marcus’s answer: virtue. The present moment. The people in front of you. The work at hand. The attempt, however imperfect, to be good.

VI. The Philosopher King

Plato dreamed of the philosopher-king, the ruler who had seen the Form of the Good and governed in its light.

Marcus Aurelius is the closest history came to making this dream real.

He was a genuine philosopher, not a dilettante who read a few books but a man who had studied Stoicism for decades, who knew the tradition deeply, who took the philosophical life seriously as a practice rather than a performance.

And he was the most powerful ruler in the world.

The result was not Plato’s ideal.

It was something more complicated and more interesting: a man who knew what he should be and struggled, daily, to be it. A man who had more power than any human being should have and used it, mostly, well. A man who wrote at night about the gap between the ideal and the real, never closed the gap, and never stopped trying.

“You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think.”

He did not leave life right now. He stayed. He governed. He wrote. He tried.

This is the philosopher-king as he actually exists. Not the serene master of the Form of the Good, but the tired man in the tent at the edge of empire, writing notes to himself by lamplight, reminding himself of what he already knows and keeps forgetting.

VII. What the Meditations Give Us

The Meditations are unlike any other philosophical text because they make no argument.

They do not try to persuade. They do not address an audience. They are not arranged for effect.

They are a man thinking, returning to the same ideas, finding slightly different formulations, testing the same principles against the specific difficulties of a specific day.

What they give us:

Permission to struggle.

Marcus was the most powerful man in the world, a devoted student of philosophy for fifty years, and he still had to remind himself, every single day, of the same basic truths.

He was still angry. Still distracted. Still afraid. Still failing to live what he knew.

If Marcus Aurelius needed daily reminders, then perhaps the philosophical life is not the achievement of a stable state but the practice of returning, again and again, to what matters.

The journal as philosophical practice.

The Meditations are, before anything else, a journal. Not a diary of events, Marcus records almost nothing that happened, but a journal of attention: where the mind went, what it found there, what it needed to be told.

The act of writing to oneself, the articulation of what you believe in the privacy of your own thought, is itself a philosophical practice. It is the examined life, practiced daily.

The ordinary life as philosophical site.

Marcus did not retire to a garden, like Epicurus. He did not die in prison, like Socrates. He ruled an empire, fought wars, managed ungrateful subordinates, attended endless administrative meetings, and found philosophy not in retreat from this but in the middle of it.

The Meditations are a record of philosophy practiced under conditions of maximum distraction, and therefore one of the most honest accounts of what philosophy actually requires.

Not the absence of difficulty. The transformation of difficulty into practice.

VIII. The Last Entry

We do not know which entry in the Meditations was last. The text is not dated.

But there is a quality to certain passages, a tiredness, a finality, a sense of summing up, that feels like late writing.

“Loss is nothing else but change, and change is Nature’s delight.”

“Accept the things to which fate binds you, and love the people with whom fate brings you together, and do so with all your heart.”

“The first rule is to keep an untroubled spirit. The second is to look things in the face and know them for what they are.”

Marcus died in 180 CE, at a military camp on the Danube, of what was probably the Antonine Plague.

He was fifty-eight years old.

By tradition, his last words, to the officer of the watch who came to ask for the password for the night, were these:

“Go to the rising sun; I am already setting.”

He had been setting for years. He had written about setting, about death, impermanence, the passage of all things, for as long as we have his writing.

When it came, he met it as he had tried to meet everything: with clarity, without pretense, and with the kind of dry wit that only a man who has fully accepted something can bring to it.

Go to the rising sun. I am already setting.

Read the Meditations in Gregory Hays’s translation, published by the Modern Library in 2002. It is the best translation in English: alive, clear, and not afraid of Marcus’s roughness.

Read it slowly, a few entries at a time.

Read it when you’re struggling, or when you’re about to do something you know is wrong.

Read it at night, alone, when the day has been difficult.

That is how it was written.

That is how it should be read.

item.title: Kant: The Man Who Never Left Königsberg and Changed Everything
item.description:
Immanuel Kant never traveled more than ten miles from his birthplace.

He was born in Königsberg, Prussia, in 1724. He studied in Königsberg, taught in Königsberg, wrote in Königsberg, and died in Königsberg in 1804.

He never married! He had no children! His daily routine was so precise that the citizens of Königsberg reportedly set their clocks by his afternoon walk. Every day, at exactly 3:30 PM, Kant would leave his house and walk the same route.

There is a story, probably apocryphal but too good not to tell, that Kant missed his walk on only two occasions in his adult life.

The first: the day he received Rousseau’s Émile. He was so absorbed he forgot to walk. :)

The second: the day news arrived of the French Revolution. He was so excited he forgot to walk. :)

Rousseau and revolution: the two things that could stop Kant’s clock.

This tells you almost everything you need to know about Immanuel Kant!

I. The Man

Let us dwell for a moment on Kant the person, because he is one of the most entertaining figures in the history of philosophy. Not because he was dramatic or scandalous, but because he was so magnificently, catastrophically boring in his personal life and so completely, utterly revolutionary in his thought.

He was small, around five feet tall. He had a slightly deformed chest, which he compensated for by an extraordinarily rigid posture and precise dress. He was obsessed with his health, developing elaborate theories about digestion, breathing, and sleep that he applied to himself with scientific rigor.

He had a theory that you should breathe only through your nose, since mouth breathing was dangerous, and he reportedly would cross the street to avoid walking behind someone who might breathe on him.

He dined with friends every day, always exactly at noon, always for exactly four hours, but had a rule that the number of guests should be at least as many as the Graces (three) and no more than the Muses (nine).

He was a brilliant conversationalist on every topic except philosophy. At dinner, he refused to discuss philosophy. He talked about science, politics, literature, travel. He was particularly interested in geography and travel writing, having never traveled anywhere himself.

His lectures were famous: witty, accessible, filled with examples. Students traveled from across Europe to attend them. His published prose was the opposite: dense, technical, relentlessly systematic, requiring multiple readings to yield meaning.

He was aware of this. He reportedly said that his Critique of Pure Reason, the most important work of philosophy written in the last 300 years, was unreadable.

He was right. It is.

Let us read it anyway.

II. The Problem Kant Was Trying to Solve

To understand what Kant did, you need to understand what was broken before him.

By the mid-18th century, European philosophy had split into two camps that could not talk to each other.

The Rationalists, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, argued that the most important truths could be known through reason alone, independent of experience. Mathematics was the model: 2 + 2 = 4 is true regardless of what you observe. The rationalists believed that God, the soul, causation, the deepest features of reality, could be demonstrated through pure reasoning.

The Empiricists, Locke, Berkeley, Hume, argued that all knowledge comes from experience. The mind at birth is a blank slate, tabula rasa. Everything we know, we learned from our senses. There are no innate ideas.

Hume took empiricism to its logical conclusion, and the conclusion was devastating.

If all knowledge comes from experience, then causation cannot be known.

You observe the billiard ball strike another and the other move. You observe this repeatedly. But you never observe the necessity of the connection, the fact that the first ball must cause the second to move. You only observe constant conjunction. The idea of necessary causal connection is not in the data. It is something the mind adds.

And if causation is just a habit of the mind, then science, which is built on causal laws, has no rational foundation.

Hume, by his own account, was left in skeptical despair.

Kant read Hume and, famously, said that Hume “awoke him from his dogmatic slumber.”

The Critique of Pure Reason (1781) is his response.

It took him eleven years to think about it. He wrote it in four to five months. The haste shows. It is one of the most disorganized great books ever written. It is also one of the most important.

III. The Copernican Revolution in Philosophy

Kant’s move was breathtaking in its audacity.

The traditional assumption: the mind conforms to objects. We perceive reality as it is because our minds accurately represent the world. Knowledge is the mind’s attempt to match reality.

Kant’s reversal: objects conform to the mind.

Not because the mind creates reality. Kant was not an idealist in that sense. But because the mind imposes a structure on experience through which all objects must be filtered before they can appear to us at all.

He called this the Copernican Revolution in philosophy.

Copernicus stopped asking why the stars move across the sky and instead asked: what if the observer is moving? The question is the same; the perspective is reversed.

Kant stopped asking how the mind comes to know reality and instead asked: what structures must the mind possess for experience to be possible at all?

The answer: space, time, and the categories of the understanding.

IV. Space and Time Are Not Out There

This is where Kant gets genuinely strange.

Space and time, for Kant, are not features of reality as it is in itself. They are the forms of intuition, the structures through which the mind organizes experience.

We do not perceive objects in space and time because space and time are properties of objects. We perceive objects in space and time because space and time are the lens through which the mind processes all sensory input.

You cannot experience anything that is not spatial and temporal because your mind cannot process anything that has not been run through the spatial-temporal filter.

This means: you will never know what reality is like independent of the structures your mind imposes on it.

The thing-in-itself, das Ding an sich, is forever inaccessible. You only ever know the phenomenon, reality as it appears through the structures of your cognition.

This is not skepticism. Kant is not saying we know nothing. He is saying: we know the phenomenal world with certainty, including scientific knowledge. But the ultimate nature of reality, noumenal reality, is beyond our grasp.

Kant’s position: we have reliable knowledge of appearances. We have no knowledge of things as they are in themselves.

The immediate implication: all the traditional metaphysics, the proofs of God’s existence, the immortality of the soul, the freedom of the will, go beyond possible experience and therefore cannot be established by theoretical reason.

Kant spent a considerable portion of the Critique systematically dismantling every metaphysical argument for God, soul, and freedom.

Then, in the Critique of Practical Reason, he argued that morality requires us to postulate them anyway.

He is the most systematic philosopher in history. He is also, in a very specific sense, a troll.

V. Synthetic A Priori Judgments

Kant introduced a distinction that has been fought over ever since.

Analytic judgments: true by definition. “All bachelors are unmarried.” The predicate is contained in the subject. These are necessarily true but tell us nothing new.

Synthetic judgments: tell us something new. “The cat is on the mat.” The predicate is not contained in the subject. These are informative but contingent.

A priori: known independently of experience. A posteriori: known through experience.

Hume assumed: analytic = a priori, synthetic = a posteriori. You either know by definition or by observation. Those are the only options.

Kant’s bombshell: there is a third category. Synthetic a priori judgments: necessarily true, known independently of experience, AND genuinely informative about the world.

His examples:

  • “7 + 5 = 12”, not true by definition (you must actually add), but necessarily true and known a priori.
  • “Every event has a cause”, not true by definition, but necessarily true and not derived from experience.
  • Geometry: “The straight line between two points is the shortest”, not contained in the concept of a straight line, but necessarily and a priori true.

These are possible, Kant argues, because they describe not reality as it is in itself but the structure the mind imposes on experience. We know that every event has a cause a priori because causation is one of the categories of the understanding, a structural feature of how the mind processes experience.

Without the category of causation, we couldn’t have coherent experience at all.

This is elegant. It is also, as Hume’s defenders point out, somewhat circular. We know causation applies to experience because causation is part of what makes experience possible. But why should we trust that the categories of our cognition track anything real?

Kant’s answer: because they are the conditions of possible experience. If they weren’t reliable for the phenomenal world, we wouldn’t have coherent experience to philosophize about.

VI. The Categorical Imperative

Kant’s ethics is, by his own standards, derived entirely from reason.

He was contemptuous of moral theories grounded in feeling, sympathy, consequences, or happiness. Not because these things don’t matter, but because they cannot ground obligation.

I might feel sympathy for you today and not tomorrow. My feelings are unreliable. If morality is grounded in feelings, morality is unreliable. But moral obligation is necessarily binding. It does not vary. Therefore, morality must be grounded in reason.

The Categorical Imperative, his supreme principle of morality, has several formulations. The most famous:

Formula of Universal Law:

“Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.”

In other words: before acting, ask: what if everyone did this?

If you are considering lying to get out of trouble, ask: what if everyone lied whenever convenient? The institution of truthful communication would collapse. Your lie depends on others telling the truth. You cannot universalize your maxim without contradiction. Therefore: do not lie.

This sounds like the Golden Rule. It is not quite the same. The Golden Rule is about reciprocity: treat others as you wish to be treated. The Categorical Imperative is about universalizability: could the principle of your action be a universal law?

Formula of Humanity:

“Act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end and never as a means only.”

This is arguably the most influential single sentence in the history of ethics.

Never use a person merely as a tool for your purposes. Every human being has a dignity, a worth that is not conditional on usefulness, that must be respected absolutely.

This grounds: the prohibition on slavery, the prohibition on torture, the prohibition on using people as experimental subjects without consent, the prohibition on treating people as statistics.

The Nuremberg Code, the Declaration of Helsinki, the entire framework of research ethics, these are Kantian in their structure, even when their authors didn’t know it.

VII. The Autonomy of the Will

Kant’s deepest ethical insight is also his most demanding.

Moral worth, for Kant, comes not from consequences, not from following God’s commands, not from social convention, but from autonomy: giving the law to yourself through reason.

Auto-nomos, self-legislating.

Take someone who behaves well only because they fear punishment. That is prudence, not morality. Someone who acts out of sympathy is being moved by emotion, not duty. Someone who simply does what their culture told them to is being conventional. Kant counts none of the three as genuine moral worth.

Moral action requires acting from the recognition that reason demands it, and choosing it for that reason alone.

This is extraordinarily demanding. It implies that most of what we call moral behavior, driven by habit, feeling, social pressure, self-interest, lacks genuine moral worth.

It also implies something Kant found important: the dignity of moral agency.

Because you are capable of autonomous moral action, because you can give the law to yourself through reason, you have a dignity that is absolutely unconditional. Not because you are useful. Not because you are loved. Because you are a rational agent, capable of autonomy.

This is the philosophical foundation of human rights.

VIII. The Things Kant Got Wrong

Now, in fairness, the places he got it wrong.

The universalizability test is underspecified.

Almost any maxim can be universalized with the right description. “Lie to murderers asking where your friends are hiding”: can this be universalized? Kant said no. Most people disagree.

The problem: the test depends heavily on how you describe the maxim. Kant’s framework does not tell you how to describe it.

The absolute prohibition on lying.

Kant famously argued that lying is always wrong, even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding.

This conclusion is so obviously wrong that generations of philosophers have proposed rescues, finding ways to interpret Kant that avoid it. Kant himself refused rescue. He meant it.

The friend knocks on your door and asks you to hide them. You lie to the murderer. And Kant says you have acted wrongly.

This is a case where the theory has clearly run ahead of the morality.

The treatment of women, non-Europeans, and animals.

Kant’s ethics grants full moral status only to rational agents. He defined rationality in ways that excluded women from full moral and political standing, a conclusion he drew explicitly and without embarrassment.

His writings on non-European peoples are worse. By his own ethical standards, treating persons as ends, his actual views about non-European peoples are not merely wrong but incoherent.

The universalist ethics and the parochial prejudices coexist in his work in a way that should make us deeply suspicious of philosophers who claim their personal limitations don’t affect their universal theories.

IX. What Kant Got Permanently Right

Despite all of that:

The critical turn: the insight that we cannot ask what reality is like without first asking what kind of knowers we are. This is still the right starting point for epistemology.

The dignity of persons: the idea that rational agents have a worth that is not conditional on usefulness or results. This is the philosophical bedrock of human rights. Whatever its origins in Kant’s specific framework, the insight survives the framework.

The autonomy of morality: the idea that moral reasons are not reducible to consequences, feelings, or commands, that morality has its own domain and its own authority. This remains, despite all the challenges, a defensible and important position.

The limits of theoretical reason: the demonstration that certain questions, God, soul, freedom, lie beyond what theoretical reason can resolve. This clears the ground for genuine intellectual humility about metaphysics.

And this:

The recognition that we are not passive receivers of reality, that the mind is active, that it structures experience, that who we are shapes what we can know.

This is not idealism. It is not relativism. It is the insistence that the knower is part of the story, that the question “what is reality like?” cannot be separated from “what kind of creature is asking?”

We are still living in the aftermath of that insight.

Coda

Kant died in 1804, aged seventy-nine, in Königsberg.

His last words, reportedly, were: “Es ist gut.”

It is good.

The man who had mapped the limits of human reason, who had grounded ethics in autonomy, who had argued that beauty required the free play of the faculties, died with a two-word verdict on the whole enterprise.

It is good.

He never left Königsberg. He changed everything anyway.

There is a lesson in that, about the relationship between movement and thought, between travel and depth, between the size of the world you inhabit and the size of the world you make.

His afternoon walk was enough!

Further reading:

Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (trans. Christine Korsgaard)

Kant, Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics (easier than the Critique)

Roger Scruton, Kant: A Very Short Introduction

Christine Korsgaard, Creating the Kingdom of Ends (1996)

Sebastian Gardner, Kant and the Critique of Pure Reason (1999)

For the brave :) : Critique of Pure Reason (trans. Norman Kemp Smith)

item.title: Why American Intellectuals Are Invisible: A Philosophical Diagnosis
item.description:
In Paris, in 1945, Jean-Paul Sartre was a celebrity.

Not a celebrity in the academic sense, not famous among philosophers and known to the educated public.

A celebrity in the full sense: recognized on the street, photographed by paparazzi, quoted in newspapers by people who had not read his books but knew his name and his positions.

His café, Les Deux Magots, was a destination. His arguments about freedom and commitment were debated in bars and kitchens by people who worked in factories and offices.

He was, in the precise sense, a public intellectual, an intellectual whose work circulated beyond the academy and entered public life as public life.

France has had a continuous tradition of these: Voltaire, Rousseau, Zola, Sartre, Beauvoir, Camus, Foucault, Derrida, Bourdieu, and their successors today.

America does not have this tradition.

America has universities. America has think tanks. America has public commentators: pundits, columnists, podcasters.

But the philosopher who shapes public moral and political imagination, the thinker whose ideas become the common vocabulary of people who have never studied philosophy, this figure is almost entirely absent from American public life.

Why?

I. Tocqueville’s Warning

The diagnosis begins in 1835.

Alexis de Tocqueville, a French aristocrat visiting America, published Democracy in America, the most perceptive account of American civilization ever written by an outsider.

He admired much. He also noticed something troubling:

“I know of no country where there is generally less independence of mind and real freedom of debate than in America.”

And more specifically:

“In America, the majority builds an impenetrable wall around thought. Within these limits, a writer is free; but woe to him who dares to go beyond them.”

Tocqueville identified what he called the tyranny of the majority, not the political tyranny of a despot, but the social tyranny of consensus:

the pressure to conform, not through legal force, but through the withdrawal of social approval, the isolation, the dismissal, the casual disregard that greets anyone who diverges too far from what most people think.

In a democracy, the majority is not only the government. The majority is the culture. And in American democracy, the majority’s opinion functions as a kind of gravity, pulling all thought toward the center, toward the practical, toward the common sense, toward what everyone already knows.

The intellectual who stands apart from this, who insists on the uncomfortable, the complex, the counterintuitive, is not persecuted.

They are simply ignored.

Tocqueville wrote this in 1835. It has not improved.

II. The Pragmatist Tradition

American philosophy has a native tradition: pragmatism.

Peirce, James, Dewey, the great American philosophical school, defined truth not as correspondence to reality but as what works.

A belief is true if it produces successful action in the world. A theory is valuable if it makes a practical difference. Philosophy must be useful. It must connect to experience, improve life, solve problems.

William James:

“The true is only the expedient in the way of our thinking, just as ‘the right’ is only the expedient in the way of our behaving.”

John Dewey:

“Philosophy recovers itself when it ceases to be a device for dealing with the problems of philosophers and becomes a method, cultivated by philosophers, for dealing with the problems of men.”

This is a genuine philosophical tradition, rich, sophisticated, influential.

But it has a cultural consequence:

It licenses the dismissal of impractical thought.

If truth is what works, if philosophy must solve the problems of ordinary life, then the philosopher who works on abstract problems with no immediate application is not merely specialized.

They are, in the pragmatist framework, doing something suspect, something that may not even be real philosophy.

The pragmatist tradition gave American culture a philosophical justification for its pre-existing suspicion of useless thinking.

III. Anti-Intellectualism as American Tradition

Richard Hofstadter won the Pulitzer Prize in 1964 for Anti-Intellectualism in American Life.

His argument: anti-intellectualism is not a deviation from American values. It is an expression of them.

Evangelical Christianity:

The revivalist tradition in American religion, from the Great Awakening through the 19th century, celebrated direct emotional experience of God over theological learning.

The learned minister was suspect. Too much education, the tradition implied, might distance you from God, might replace faith with argument, experience with abstraction.

The revivalist preacher who spoke from the gut, from the heart, from direct access to the Holy Spirit, this was the American religious ideal.

Not the theologian.

Jacksonian democracy:

Andrew Jackson’s presidency (1829-1837) celebrated the “common man” against the educated elite.

The expert was suspect. The professional was suspect. The man of learning was suspect.

What was trusted: practical experience, common sense, the wisdom of ordinary people doing ordinary things.

This is not merely political rhetoric. It is a deep American cultural value, the suspicion that too much learning corrupts the natural good sense that ordinary Americans possess.

The business culture:

American capitalism produced a specific ideal: the self-made man, the entrepreneur who created value through practical ingenuity, not through inherited knowledge or academic credentials.

Carnegie. Rockefeller. Ford. Edison.

None of them had advanced degrees. All of them were celebrated as quintessentially American, their lack of academic formation not a deficiency but a virtue, proof that real intelligence is practical, that real success comes from doing, not from thinking.

The businessman became the American hero.

The intellectual, who thinks without building, who criticizes without creating, who questions without solving, became, in this cultural framework, a suspicious figure.

Parasitic on productive society. Too clever to be trusted. Too abstract to be useful.

IV. The Frankfurt School’s American Experience

In the 1930s and 1940s, some of the greatest European intellectuals fled to America.

The Frankfurt School, Adorno, Horkheimer, Marcuse, Fromm, landed in New York and California.

They brought with them a tradition of critical theory: the analysis of culture, ideology, and capitalism using a synthesis of Marx, Freud, and Hegel.

They encountered something they had not expected.

Not persecution. Not censorship.

Indifference.

Adorno, in California, studying the culture industry, watching American popular culture absorb everything:

“The culture industry perpetually cheats its consumers of what it perpetually promises. The promissory note which, with its plots and staging, it draws on pleasure is endlessly prolonged.”

What Adorno observed: American culture was extraordinary at absorbing criticism, at commodifying dissent, at packaging the radical as entertainment, at neutralizing the dangerous by making it popular.

The critic who attacked consumer culture found their books in the consumer culture’s bookstores. The philosopher who critiqued the spectacle found themselves on the spectacle’s television.

The system was not hostile to ideas. It was indifferent to them, which is worse.

You cannot fight indifference. It does not argue back. It simply does not engage.

Marcuse stayed. He became influential in the 1960s counterculture. One-Dimensional Man became a student movement text.

Adorno and Horkheimer returned to Germany.

They could not find, in America, the public they needed, the audience that would take ideas seriously as ideas, not as consumer products or political tools.

V. The Structural Problem: the University and the Public

In Europe, the university professor has traditionally had a public role.

The French normalien, graduate of the École Normale Supérieure, was expected to engage in public debate, to write for general audiences, to take positions on political and moral questions.

The German professor, holder of an academic chair, was a public figure, whose expertise carried cultural authority beyond the seminar room.

In America, the university was shaped differently.

The research university model (post-Civil War):

The American research university, modeled partly on the German university but modified by American conditions, made the production of specialized knowledge its primary purpose.

The professor’s job: to produce research, to train graduate students, to advance a discipline.

Its purpose was not to form citizens, or to engage the public, or to take part in the Öffentlichkeit, the public sphere, the way European academics were expected to.

The publish-or-perish system rewarded narrow specialization.

The professor who wrote for general audiences was spending time that should be spent on peer-reviewed publications. The professor who engaged in public debate was doing something that counted for nothing in the tenure file.

The system actively discouraged the public intellectual role.

The disciplinary fragmentation:

American academia became intensely specialized.

The philosopher of language. The historian of 14th-century Catalonia. The economist specializing in labor markets in sub-Saharan Africa.

Each field has its journals, its conferences, its internal debates, conducted in a technical vocabulary inaccessible to outsiders.

The intellectual who crosses boundaries, who writes about ethics AND politics AND economics AND culture simultaneously, is suspect in every discipline. Not specialist enough to be trusted, not rigorous enough to be cited. Writing for a general audience is taken as evidence that you are not serious.

VI. France vs. America: the Structural Difference

Why does France produce public intellectuals and America does not?

The French grandes écoles:

The École Normale Supérieure, Sciences Po, the École Polytechnique. These institutions train a small elite that is expected to move between disciplines, between academia and journalism, between theory and practice.

The normalien is not a specialist. They are an intellectual, full stop. Expected to have views on everything and to express them publicly.

This tradition is institutional. It is reproduced deliberately.

The French intellectual press:

Le Monde, Le Figaro, Libération, Le Nouvel Observateur. French newspapers and magazines print philosophical and cultural essays at length, by academics, for general audiences.

The essay form, the intellectual essay, has a home in French journalism.

American newspapers do not print 3,000-word essays on the nature of power by philosophy professors.

They print op-eds. 800 words. Accessible. Practical. Immediately relevant. Not what Sartre wrote.

The café culture:

This is perhaps too romantic, but not entirely wrong.

The Parisian café as intellectual space, where ideas circulate between academics, writers, journalists, students, and interested citizens, has no American equivalent.

The American equivalent is the university seminar. Closed. Credentialed. Inaccessible.

The café is public. The seminar is private.

VII. The American Exceptions, and What They Reveal

America has had public intellectuals.

The New York Intellectuals (1930s-1960s):

Lionel Trilling, Irving Howe, Philip Rahv, Mary McCarthy, Edmund Wilson, Hannah Arendt, writing in Partisan Review, Commentary, The New York Review of Books.

Genuinely public: they wrote about literature, politics, philosophy, culture for educated general audiences.

Genuinely intellectual: they took ideas seriously as ideas, not as tools.

Why did they exist? Several reasons.

They were mostly outsiders, Jewish intellectuals at the margins of WASP cultural institutions, with less investment in academic respectability.

They wrote in magazines that paid for serious ideas.

They had a specific audience: the educated non-academic who read seriously but was not in the university.

They were possible because of specific historical conditions. Those conditions no longer obtain.

Noam Chomsky:

The most widely read American intellectual globally, cited, translated, influential in every country except his own.

In America: marginalized, dismissed as a crank, virtually absent from mainstream media.

The contrast is instructive. Chomsky’s ideas travel everywhere except home, because his criticism of American power is exactly the kind of thought that the tyranny of American consensus makes invisible.

Not censored. Marginalized. There is a difference. Marginalization is more effective.

Cornel West:

Genuinely public, genuinely intellectual, appears on television, engages popular culture, writes for general audiences.

But note: West is a Black intellectual in the tradition of Du Bois, a tradition that was public by necessity, because the Black intellectual could not retreat into the white academy and could not afford to be invisible in public life.

The Black public intellectual tradition is one of the few genuine public intellectual traditions in American life, produced by exclusion from the private academy and urgency about the public stakes.

VIII. The Internet, Promise and Failure

The internet seemed to promise a new public sphere.

Substack, podcasts, YouTube, the dismantling of the gatekeepers who kept intellectuals invisible.

The promise has been partially kept.

There are serious thinkers building genuine audiences online. Tyler Cowen, Scott Alexander, Freddie deBoer, Agnes Callard, people doing real intellectual work and reaching real audiences.

But the internet has also reproduced the American pathologies at scale:

The platform replaces the argument. The number of subscribers is the measure of seriousness.

The practical drives out the theoretical. The most successful online intellectuals write about productivity, money, relationships, the pragmatic concerns of daily life. The philosopher of consciousness has fewer readers than the life coach.

Speed replaces depth. The newsletter must come out weekly. The podcast must come out daily. The thinking must fit the production schedule.

The internet gave intellectuals a platform. It gave them the platform on the platform’s terms.

The terms are American terms: practical, accessible, frequent, engaging.

Not wrong terms. But not sufficient for the kind of thinking that France produces.

IX. What America Loses

The invisibility of American intellectuals is not merely a cultural aesthetic failure. It has concrete consequences.

Policy without theory:

American policy debates are conducted in the language of pragmatism: what works, what is practical, what can be sold to voters.

The deeper questions, what kind of society do we want to be, what values should animate our institutions, what is the philosophical basis of our rights, are conducted without philosophers.

Policy is made without philosophy.

This produces policy that is technically sophisticated and philosophically incoherent, that can optimize for metrics without being able to ask whether the metrics measure what matters.

Democracy without citizens:

Tocqueville’s fear was not merely cultural. It was political.

Democracy requires citizens who think, who can evaluate arguments, who have the intellectual resources to participate in self-governance, who cannot be easily manipulated by the confident and the visible.

The invisible intellectual leaves a vacuum.

The vacuum is filled by the pundit, the influencer, the demagogue: the visible without the knowledge, the confident without the expertise.

The colonization by expertise from elsewhere:

When Americans want philosophical frameworks, they import them.

Rawls is an exception, but Rawls is read more carefully in Europe than in American policy discussions.

Foucault, Habermas, Bourdieu, Rancière, the frameworks that educated Americans use to think about power, justice, culture, are largely European.

America has exported its practical knowledge. It has imported its theoretical frameworks.

This is an intellectual trade deficit with specific structural causes.

X. The Foucault-Chomsky Debate: a Case Study in Visibility

In November 1971, Dutch television broadcast a debate between Michel Foucault and Noam Chomsky.

Two hours. Two of the greatest living thinkers. On human nature, power, justice, and the state.

In the Netherlands, it was a television event. In France, it was discussed for years. Across Europe, it became a reference point, a moment in the public intellectual tradition that people cited, argued about, returned to.

In America: almost unknown until it was uploaded to YouTube decades later.

The debate is extraordinary.

Foucault and Chomsky disagree on almost everything: on human nature (Chomsky believes in it, Foucault is skeptical), on the foundation of justice (Chomsky appeals to natural rights, Foucault argues all justice claims are themselves expressions of power), on the role of the intellectual in political struggle.

But they agree on one thing: that these questions matter, that they are worth two hours of television, that the public deserves to think about them.

Imagine this on American television in 1971. Or in 2024.

It is not imaginable.

Not because Americans could not follow it. Because the system that produces American television has no category for it.

It isn’t news, and it isn’t entertainment, and it certainly isn’t practical. It does not tell you how to live better, make more money, lose weight, or understand what happened today.

It is two people thinking in public.

This, thinking in public, is precisely what American television has never been able to accommodate.

The flaneur and the hustle:

Baudelaire’s flaneur, the wanderer, the observer of the city, the person who has nowhere to be and therefore sees everything, is a distinctly European figure.

The flaneur requires something American culture has never accepted as a legitimate use of time:

purposeless presence.

The flaneur isn’t being productive, or networking, or optimizing. They are simply walking, watching, thinking.

This is, in the American framework, waste.

“Time is money”, Benjamin Franklin, the founding pragmatist, said this in 1748.

It became the organizing principle of a civilization.

If time is money, the flaneur is spending money for no return. The philosopher thinking useless thoughts is wasting capital. The intellectual debating justice on television is two hours of productivity that will never be recovered.

The European city, Paris, Berlin, Vienna, was built for the flaneur: cafés where you can sit for three hours with one coffee, squares designed for wandering, a public life that accommodates the person who has no destination.

The American city, with exceptions, was built for productivity: the grid, the car, the suburb, the destination always predetermined, the wandering designed out.

You cannot be a flaneur in a city that was built against flanerie.

You cannot be a public intellectual in a culture that was built against purposeless thought.

XI. The Possibility of Change

I want to end with what is possible, not what is probable.

The conditions for American public intellectuals:

A public intellectual requires:

  1. An audience, people who want serious ideas, who are not satisfied by entertainment disguised as thought.

  2. A medium, a publication, a platform, that will sustain long-form serious work without requiring it to be immediately practical.

  3. Institutional support, or freedom from institutional pressure, the ability to think across disciplines without career penalty.

  4. A tradition, the sense that this is a legitimate role, that the philosopher-in-public is not wasting their time.

None of these is impossible. All of them are structurally undermined by current American conditions.

The reason for cautious hope:

The conditions that made the New York Intellectuals possible, outsiders with no stake in academic respectability, specific magazines that paid for serious work, a moment of genuine political urgency, can, in different forms, recur.

The political urgency is present. The outsiders exist: in the margins of the academy, in the new online platforms, in the communities that have always been excluded from the comfortable consensus.

The question is whether the specific American aversion to useless thinking, the pragmatist inheritance, the Jacksonian suspicion, the tyranny of the majority, can be overcome by the urgency of the current moment.

Tocqueville thought it could not. He may have been right.

He may also have been describing the structural condition rather than the permanent condition, the features of a young democracy that could, in time, mature into something more willing to tolerate the uncomfortable, the abstract, the useless.

We are still waiting.

Coda

Baudrillard is known in France. In America, he is known to people who took a theory course in college and remember the word “simulacrum.”

This is not because Americans are less intelligent. It is because America built a civilization in which the question Baudrillard asked, what is real, and how do we know?, was, for most of American history, less urgent than the question: what works, and how do we build it?

A young country building itself from wilderness to superpower in two hundred years did not have much use for Baudrillard.

It had use for engineers. For lawyers. For entrepreneurs. For soldiers.

The thinker who questions the foundations, who asks whether what we are building is worth building, whether the real is real, whether the common sense is sense, this thinker is useful when the building is done.

America is not sure the building is done.

It may never be!

And so the philosopher waits, visible to everyone in Europe, invisible at home, still asking the questions that a civilization in a hurry does not have time to hear…

P.S. : Some people felt I was being a bit unfair to pragmatism. You’re right!

That’s what happens when you isolate one point and put it under the microscope in a single piece: it can start to look like I’m singling it out as the culprit. There is, of course, a valid point in what you’re saying though: pragmatism is a useful key for understanding American anti-intellectualism. But when it’s placed alone in the defendant’s chair, it may have come across as a bit too reductive. This is my promise to my readers:

I’ll come back to pragmatism and try to make myself better understood.

Warmly!

Further reading:

Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835), Part II, Volume II for the cultural analysis.

Hofstadter, Anti-Intellectualism in American Life (1963), the essential historical account.

Jacoby, The Last Intellectuals (1987), on the disappearance of American public intellectuals.

Adorno & Horkheimer, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944), the Frankfurt School’s American diagnosis.

Dewey, The Public and Its Problems (1927), pragmatism’s attempt at a public philosophy.

Gramsci, Prison Notebooks, on organic vs. traditional intellectuals, essential for understanding the American case.

Bourdieu, The Field of Cultural Production (1993), the sociology of intellectual visibility.

Chomsky, Manufacturing Consent (1988), on media and intellectual marginalization.

item.title: Plato — The Cave, the Sun, and the Man Who Chose to Die
item.description:
There is a cave.

Inside the cave, prisoners sit chained, facing a wall. Behind them, a fire burns. Between the fire and the prisoners, people walk carrying objects: statues of animals, figures, things.

The shadows of these objects fall on the wall.

The prisoners have been here since birth. They have never seen the fire. They have never seen the objects. They have seen only the shadows.

For them, the shadows are reality. They have names for the shadows. They have expertise in predicting which shadow will appear next. They compete with each other in this expertise. They are proud of what they know.

Then one prisoner is freed.

He turns. He sees the fire, blinding, painful. He is dragged upward, out of the cave, into the sunlight.

He cannot see at first. Everything is too bright, too real, too much. Gradually, he adjusts. He sees the actual objects. He sees the actual world. He sees, finally, the sun itself, the source of all light, all visibility, all truth.

He goes back into the cave.

He tries to tell the others what he has seen.

They do not believe him. His eyes, readjusted to the dark, can no longer predict the shadows as well as they once could.

They think the journey has made him stupid.

If they could, they would kill him.

I. Plato and the Shape of Western Thought

Plato was born in Athens around 428 BCE.

Alfred North Whitehead, the mathematician and philosopher, wrote that the history of Western philosophy is “a series of footnotes to Plato.”

It is not hyperbole, and barely even a metaphor.

Every major question Western philosophy has ever asked, Plato asked first: what is real, what is knowledge, what is justice, what is beauty, what the good life is, how we should organize ourselves, what the relationship is between the particular and the universal. He asked first, and answered with a systematic completeness that has shaped the terms of the debate ever since.

He didn’t just ask questions. He invented the dialogue as a philosophical form: philosophy as conversation, as thinking together rather than handing down conclusions.

He founded the Academy, the first institution of higher learning in the Western world, which ran for over nine hundred years, until the Emperor Justinian closed it in 529 CE.

And he had a teacher whose death shaped everything he wrote.

II. Socrates — The Man Who Knew Nothing

Socrates wrote nothing.

Everything we know about him comes from others: mostly Plato, but also Xenophon and Aristophanes. The Socrates of Plato’s dialogues may or may not be the historical Socrates; scholars have argued about it for centuries.

What is clear: Socrates was a man who walked the streets of Athens asking questions.

Not rhetorical ones, and not questions he secretly had the answers to. Questions he genuinely did not know the answer to, or claimed not to.

He asked generals what courage was. He asked politicians what justice was. He asked poets what beauty was.

In every case, the person he asked began in confidence and ended in confusion, their assumed knowledge dissolved under the patient, relentless pressure of his questioning.

This method, elenchus, refutation, wasn’t meant to humiliate. It was meant to reveal something: that what we think we know, we very often don’t know at all.

The Oracle at Delphi had declared Socrates the wisest man in Athens. Socrates tested the claim by going to talk to people who were assumed to be wise. His conclusion:

“I know that I know nothing, and in this I am wiser than those who think they know but do not.”

This is where philosophy begins: not in the possession of answers, but in the honest confrontation with ignorance.

The Athenians found this intolerable.

III. The Allegory of the Cave — A Close Reading

The Allegory of the Cave appears in Book VII of The Republic, Plato’s most ambitious work, a dialogue about justice that turns into a dialogue about everything.

The cave is not a metaphor for ignorance in the simple sense, for not knowing facts. It is a metaphor for the structure of ordinary consciousness, for the way we all, inevitably, mistake appearance for reality, shadow for substance.

The prisoners are not stupid. They are us.

Their mistake isn’t a failure of intelligence. It is a failure of position. They are chained in a way that keeps them from seeing the sources of what they see. They see effects without causes, appearances without the things that cast them.

The shadows on the wall correspond, in Plato’s framework, to the world of ordinary experience, the world of particular, changing, impermanent things that we take in through the senses.

The objects carried in front of the fire correspond to the mathematical and scientific objects: more real than the shadows, but still dependent on the fire (the intellect) that lights them up.

The sunlit world outside the cave corresponds to the realm of the Forms, the perfect, eternal, unchanging archetypes of which everything in the sensory world is an imperfect copy.

The sun itself corresponds to the Form of the Good, the highest Form, the source of all being and all knowability, which Plato, in some passages, identifies with God.

This is the Theory of Forms, Plato’s most radical and most contested contribution to philosophy.

IV. The Theory of Forms

Consider a circle.

You have seen many circles: drawn on paper, traced in sand, bent out of wire. None of them is a perfect circle. Every drawn circle has its imperfections: slight irregularities, a width to the line, a physical body that falls short of the ideal.

But you know what a perfect circle is. You can recognize that drawn circles approximate it. You can measure how far they fall short.

So where is this perfect circle? It isn’t in the physical world; it has no physical instance anywhere. It isn’t in any single mind either; it isn’t just a private impression.

For Plato, it lives in the realm of Forms, a non-physical, non-mental realm of perfect, eternal objects that the physical world only ever imperfectly copies.

The Form of Circle is more real than any drawn circle, because it is what every drawn circle is trying to be, what makes it a circle and not a squiggle.

Extend this to everything.

The Form of Beauty, which beautiful things imperfectly copy. The Form of Justice, which just acts imperfectly instantiate. The Form of the Good, the highest Form, which lights up all the others the way the sun lights up the physical world.

Mathematical objects, numbers and geometric figures, are the clearest examples of Forms. Seven is not a physical object. It is not in anyone’s head. It is necessarily what it is, eternally, unchangeably, and in Plato’s sense it is more real than any seven apples you could line up on a table.

This is the part I can’t read from a comfortable distance, because I have spent a serious chunk of my life inside a small version of it. I play Go. And anyone who plays seriously knows the feeling: in any given position there is a best move, and it is there whether or not you ever find it. You don’t invent it. You uncover it, sometimes after staring at the board for ten minutes, sometimes not at all. The move was always already the best move. Your blindness to it changes nothing.

So I’ll admit my bias outright: I think mathematics is discovered, not invented. The best move in a position was the best move before anyone ever sat down to play it. That feeling, that you are walking toward something already real rather than building it, is the whole Platonic pull, and I have never once been able to resist it.

The philosopher’s task, the freed prisoner’s task, is to turn away from the shadows and follow the hard path upward: toward knowledge of the Forms, and finally toward the Good itself.

V. Why the Philosopher Must Return

The freed prisoner goes back.

This is the move that separates Plato’s philosopher from the mystic or the pure contemplative.

Having seen the sun, having reached the highest knowledge, the philosopher does not stay up in the light. They go back into the cave. They try to govern, to educate, to lead.

And not because the cave is pleasant. It isn’t, and they will be mocked for coming back, maybe killed for it. They return because justice requires it.

In The Republic, the philosopher-king, the one who has reached knowledge of the Good, is obligated to put that knowledge in the service of the community.

The highest knowledge is not private. It is political. It creates obligation.

This is one of the most contested claims in all of Plato.

Some readers find it authoritarian. Who decides who the philosopher-kings are? Who guards the guardians?

Others find it the only coherent answer to the problem of political legitimacy: rule should be in the hands of those who actually know, not the wealthy or the popular or the well-born, but those who have genuinely understood the Good.

The Republic never resolves the tension. Neither does political philosophy in general. It is one of the permanent problems of the relationship between knowledge and power.

VI. The Death of Socrates

In 399 BCE, Socrates was put on trial.

The charges: impiety (not believing in the gods of the city) and corrupting the youth of Athens.

The trial was political. Socrates had been associated with figures on the losing side of the recent civil conflict, including Critias, one of the brutal Thirty Tyrants.

The jury: 501 Athenian citizens. The vote: 280 to 221 for conviction.

He was given the chance to propose an alternative penalty.

He proposed that Athens should pay him a salary for his service to the city.

The jury, unamused, voted for death: 360 to 141.

He was sentenced to drink hemlock, a poison that causes a slow paralysis, working its way upward from the feet.

He had the chance to escape. His friends arranged it. He refused.

The Crito, one of Plato’s most powerful dialogues, records his reasons.

He had lived his whole life in Athens. He had accepted the benefits of Athenian law. To escape now would be to break the implicit contract between a citizen and the laws of his city, to act as if the laws applied only when convenient, which would dissolve the entire basis of law.

He would not do it.

He drank the hemlock.

The Phaedo records his last hours: a philosophical conversation with his friends about the immortality of the soul.

Socrates argues, with his usual mix of intellectual rigor and personal calm, that the philosopher should not fear death, that the whole philosophical life is a preparation for death, a long practice of separating the soul from the body, of choosing the eternal over the temporary.

His last words, to his friend Crito:

“Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius. Pay it and do not neglect it.”

Asclepius was the god of healing. A cock was offered to him in gratitude for recovery from illness.

Socrates, dying, was giving thanks: for recovery from the illness of life, for the healing that death brings to a soul that has spent its whole life seeking truth.

Whether you find this beautiful or chilling depends on what you think about the soul.

What’s undeniable is that the man died the way he had lived. Without fear, without pretense, still tending to the small obligations even at the last moment.

VII. What the Cave Gets Right

The Allegory of the Cave is not science. The Theory of Forms is not, in any straightforward sense, true, at least not the way Plato meant it.

But the cave gets something permanently right.

We do not see reality directly.

We see appearances, filtered through our senses, our concepts, our language, the particular architecture of our brains.

The history of science is largely the history of discovering that the obvious is wrong. That the sun does not go around the earth. That solid matter is mostly empty space. That the act of looking changes the thing you look at.

That last one has haunted me since I first really understood quantum mechanics, and it is the cave almost exactly: a century of quantum mechanics spent learning that we never get to see the thing itself, only the shadow it throws when we measure it. (I wrote about that problem on its own elsewhere. It is the cave, with equations.) Plato would have recognized the shape of it on sight.

The cave catches something that naive realism, the idea that we simply see the world as it is, cannot account for.

Education is not the filling of an empty vessel.

Plato’s image of education, the turning of the whole person toward the light, is still the most profound account of what real learning takes.

It isn’t the acquisition of information. It is the reorientation of attention, the slow growth of new ways of seeing, the willingness to be disoriented by something more real than what you were used to.

Knowledge creates obligation.

The philosopher who goes back into the cave, knowledge as the beginning of responsibility rather than an excuse from it, is still one of the strongest arguments against the idea that intellectual life is purely private.

If you see more clearly, you owe something to those who do not yet see.

What you owe, exactly, is the hardest question.

VIII. The Permanent Socratic Question

Socrates did not die for a doctrine, or for the theory of Forms, or for a proof that the soul is immortal.

He died for a practice: the practice of examining life, of refusing to accept unexamined assumptions, of following an argument wherever it leads no matter the social cost.

“The unexamined life is not worth living.”

This sentence, from the Apology, Socrates’s speech at his trial, is the most provocative sentence in Western philosophy.

Provocative not because it is obviously true, but because it is so obviously debatable, and the debate it starts is itself a piece of the examined life it is recommending.

Is the examined life better than the unexamined one? What counts as examination? Is the peasant who never reads a word of philosophy but lives with integrity and love living an unexamined life?

Socrates would have enjoyed these questions. He would have had no final answers.

He would have kept asking.

That, for him, was the point.

IX. Plato’s Shadow on Everything

Plato never really leaves.

Every time you separate appearance from reality, you are doing something Platonic.

Every time you catch yourself believing that mathematics is discovered rather than invented, that the Pythagorean theorem was true before anyone proved it, that the best move in a position was the best move before anyone found it, you are a Platonist about mathematics. (I am, without apology. See above.)

Every time you feel that justice is not simply whatever the powerful decide, that there is a standard the powerful themselves can be measured against, you are reaching for something like the Form of Justice.

Plato isn’t a historical curiosity. He is the shape of certain ways of thinking we still haven’t found a way to abandon, because they catch something true about how we actually deal with truth, with value, with the world.

Even the people who reject him hardest, Aristotle, Nietzsche, the logical positivists, are defined by the rejection. You cannot escape Plato. You only get to choose your relationship to him.

Start with the Apology, Socrates’s speech at his trial.

Then the Phaedo, his last hours :’(.

Then the Republic, if you have the patience for it. It will repay you beyond almost any book I know.

The Allegory of the Cave is Book VII, but read Books I through VI first.

The cave means more once you know what came before it.

item.title: Yaşamaya Değer Mi?
item.description:
Camus, Sisifos Söyleni‘ne şöyle başlar:

“Gerçekten ciddi olan tek felsefi soru vardır: intihar.”

İlk okuduğumda ürkmüştüm.

Sonra anladım ki bu bir davet değil. Bir test! Yaşamaya neden devam ettiğini bilmiyorsan, zaten yaşamıyorsun demektir.

Sürükleniyorsun.

Seneca ise yüzyıllar önce şunu yazmıştı: “Omnia aliena sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est.” Her şey başkasına ait, yalnızca zaman bizimdir.

İkisi de aynı şeyi söylüyor aslında, farklı kapılardan. Camus anlam soruyor. Seneca zaman soruyor. Ama her ikisinin altında aynı soru yatıyor:

Sen neredesin, şu an?

Absürd dediğimiz şey; dünyanın anlamsızlığı değil, bizim anlam arayışımızla dünyanın sessizliğinin çarpışması. Sisifos kayayı yukarı taşıyor, kaya aşağı yuvarlanıyor. Camus diyor ki: Sisifos’u mutlu hayal etmeliyiz.

Bu bana çok şey ifade etti bir dönem. Anlam bulunmaz, yapılır. Taşı taşımak bile, bilinçli taşınırsa, bir cevaptır.

Seneca ise saatlerimizi, günlerimizi, yıllarımızı sayıyor. “Ne kadar zamanın var?” diye sormuyor — “Ne kadar zamanın kaldı?” diye soruyor.

Belki de doğru soru şu: Sisifos’un ellerinde nasıl bir kalem olurdu? :)

(Ters köșeeee, en bi sevdiğimmmm.)

Ve tepeye çıkarken ne yazardı?
